## 2026-08-13 — mok_like trains on the fabric transport at EP4

Three steps at four ranks, one process per GPU, `State: succeeded`, 9.7 s/it at one layer, and the
distributed contract passing with zero generation mismatches and zero slot-reuse failures. Four
defects stood between the last update and that run, each hidden behind the one before it.

### The illegal address was peer XLA reads under a cross-process transport

The fault that blocked the training path all along is a configuration guard asking the wrong
question. `MokLikeConfig` already rejected the direct-read storage modes when they cannot reach a
peer, but keyed the check on the expert group outgrowing one node:

```python
if self.requires_cross_process_transport:   # num_devices > 4
```

A four-rank group under `FABRIC_SYMMETRIC` runs one process per GPU, so it crosses processes at
`num_devices == 4` and passed the guard. `MokLikeForwardXStorage.XLA_PEER_EXPERIMENTAL` then had
the megakernel read each peer's `x` straight out of that peer's XLA buffer. Across processes that
address belongs to another process and only the arena is mapped, and `Acquire` fills
`forward_x_ptrs[rank]` for the local rank alone under the arena-mode rendezvous mask, so three of
the four pointers handed to `dispatch_kernel` were never populated. The guard's comment already
stated the right rule — the direct-read modes "stay process-local whatever the transport does" —
so the fix keys it on `workspace_transport.crosses_processes`, and the launcher stages forward `x`
whenever the transport crosses processes rather than failing every preset-based fabric run.

`PROMOTED_DROPLESS_V12` selects `XLA_PEER_EXPERIMENTAL`; every probe on this branch used
runtime-staged `x`, which lives in the arena. That is why the kernel-level and model-level gates
all passed while only the training path faulted, and it retires the open question from the previous
update rather than adding another elimination to it.

### Three more behind it

**Sharded autotuning deadlocked the compile.** With the forward fixed, all four ranks parked in
`backend_compile_and_load` at zero CPU across 1142 threads. Sharded autotuning splits the search
across processes and exchanges results through the coordination service, which a process-per-GPU
group never completes. `--xla_gpu_shard_autotuning=false` compiles the same step in about twelve
seconds; the launcher now sets it whenever the transport crosses processes. A Python stack alone
was misleading here -- a blocked C++ call looks exactly like a working one, and only the CPU
measurement separated them.

**`train_step_result` was never bound.** The trim helper takes the whole step result so it can wait
on it before releasing pool memory, but the call site unpacked the tuple and passed a name that did
not exist, so the first completed step raised `NameError`. Introduced on this branch, not on main.

**The debug-counter read walked absent ranks.** `ReadDebugCounters` indexed `runtimes_` by rank and
called `cudaSetDevice(rank)`. Under the fabric transport the process holds one rank at storage
index 0 behind a single visible GPU, so the walk ran off a one-element vector and handed
`cudaMemcpy` a pointer that segfaulted in `cuMemcpyDtoH_v2`. It now reads only the ranks the
process owns, which is what the caller already assumed: it sums locally and allgathers one summary
per process.

**The handler-call contract assumed one process owned every rank.** `steps * layers * 4` holds for
the sealed in-process layout. Under fabric each process owns one rank, so a correct three-step run
reported three calls against an expectation of twelve and failed its own contract. It now scales by
`jax.local_device_count()`.

### What made it findable

Two error-reporting defects were hiding the cause, both fixed here.

The forward and backward handlers caught the real failure as `exc`, then reported only the error
raised while closing it:

```cpp
} catch (const std::exception& closure_error) {
  TerminalCudaFailure(std::string("could not close a rank-local forward failure: ")
                      + closure_error.what());
```

A device trap poisons the CUDA context, so every later call returns the same sticky
illegal-access error. Every run therefore reported `PublishCancellationKernel: an illegal memory
access was encountered` — the cleanup path failing — and discarded the only description of what
went wrong. With `exc.what()` restored and `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1` forwarded through the grug
dispatcher, the message became `cudaLaunchKernelEx(MoK forward): an illegal memory access was
encountered`, which placed the fault inside the megakernel at `ordinal=0`.

`MOK_TRACE_INVOCATIONS` prints each reservation (`rank / run / collective / phase / ordinal / slot
/ generation`) and the per-invocation shapes against the arena sizing. Both are behind the env var
and off by default.

### Retracted

Two claims from the previous update do not survive.

**The arena-mode slot release is not a regression.** `ReleaseAfterStream` enqueues `Complete()`
through `cudaLaunchHostFunc` behind the `WaitCompletionKernel` that spins until every peer has
stamped the generation, so reaching `FinishRankLocked` already proves on device that no peer is
still reading the slot. Releasing on the local rank alone is correct; the in-process path waits for
all ranks only because one manager owns them and each reports separately. Recorded in the code,
since the reasoning is not local to the branch.

**Reservation order is not diverging.** All four ranks report `ordinal=0 slot=0 generation=2` for
the first forward.

### Eliminated by measurement

- **Remat inside the layer scan.** `lax.scan` over stacked per-layer parameters with
  `eqx.filter_checkpoint` applied per iteration, forward and backward, differentiating both
  activations and parameters, passes cross-process on four ranks. This was the last structural
  difference between the probes and the training path.
- **Schedule capacity.** `schedule_capacity` is 1,052,672 against an arena receive region of
  `num_tokens * top_k` = 262,144, a ratio of 4.0 that comes from
  `STRICT_WORST_CASE_FOUR_RANK_SCHEDULE_CAPACITY_FACTOR`. Running at 1.1 gives 290,816 and faults
  identically, so the mismatch is not the trigger. The megakernel documents
  `y_routed_recv_buffer` as `(num_local_tokens * topk, H)`, which the arena provides.
- **Macrobatch alignment.** 1,052,672 is not a multiple of `macrobatch_size` 32,768 and the host
  validates only `minibatch_size`, but the kernel bounds each macrobatch with
  `min(macrobatch_size, num_tokens - macrobatch_offset)`, so the tail is handled.

### Not yet measured

The single-node gate is a correctness result, not a performance one. No MFU, throughput, or drop
rate yet, and no matched comparison against the ra2a arm; 25-step runs of both arms are in flight.
EP64, multi-rack, and the #8236 evaluation remain untouched.

## 2026-08-13 — mok_like trains at EP64 on one rack

Sixty-four ranks across sixteen nodes, one process per GPU, fabric transport, `State: succeeded`:

```
Progress on:train 3.00it/3.00it  rate:7.7s/it  loss=9.28
mok_like runtime completed with 1162 recorded peer waits and 6 handlers per phase/process
```

`6 handlers per phase/process` is three steps times two layers times the one rank each process owns,
so the workspace protocol is right at sixty-four ranks rather than merely not faulting. The fabric
handle exchange now works across hosts, which is the reason the transport exists.

### The launcher had never expressed an EP64 mesh

`expert_axis_size` was pinned to the per-node GPU count with `replica_axis_size = num_nodes`, so a
one-rack run was EP4 x DP16. The expert axis now follows the requested group when it outgrows a
node and the replica axis takes what is left; every existing arm keeps its previous mesh. Two more
gaps sat behind that: `MokLikeBuildConfig` never received `num_devices`, so a sixty-four-process job
asked the rendezvous to assemble a four-rank group, and the matched shape's eight experts cannot
divide over an axis of sixty-four, so the expert count is now a parameter checked against the axis.

### Three hardcoded rank counts

Each was invisible until a real sixty-four-rank run.

- **FFI registration.** `register_ffi_targets` took its four-rank default, so a sixty-four-rank
  library was asked for `levanter_mok_forward_bf16_4`. The handler symbols are rank-suffixed. The
  test now records the count it was asked to register.
- **Debug-counter ABI.** The per-rank stride is seven scalars, one phase-by-peer block for each of
  wait events, cycles, and max cycles, then four staging tallies -- `11 + 12N`, so 59 at four ranks
  and 779 at sixty-four. Both the expected total and the unpacking offsets were the constants they
  take at four, so the run read 49856 values as 236 and died before reporting anything.
- **Autotune cache.** The per-fusion cache directory is chosen per node, but the fabric transport
  puts four processes on a node, so they shared a temp directory and raced. Two ranks died on
  `NOT_FOUND` for an entry another process had already moved.

### Diagnosis at rack scale

Sixty-four ranks flood the log service past its line cap, and what survives is coordination-teardown
noise. Both rack failures were diagnosed from the per-rank tracebacks written to object storage
instead. That path was itself broken -- `marin_prefix()` carries no trailing separator, so
concatenating a relative path wrote sixty-four tracebacks to a sibling of the prefix that nothing
reads. It now uses `prefix_join`.

### Not yet measured at rack scale

The full matched shape does not fit: forty-eight layers at 192 experts raises
`RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED: Out of memory while trying to allocate 147.83GiB` inside `jit_train_step`.
Part of that is self-inflicted by the comparison shape -- the hero fits at this scale using latent
compression and asymmetric routed/shared widths, and the fused kernel forces both off. A reduced
depth run is in flight for a rack-scale MFU number.

### The one change that unblocks the rest

Shared-expert de-fusing. The megakernel reads `intermediate_dim` off `shared_gate.dimensions()[0]`
and takes a single `x` for routed and shared experts, which is why the comparison pins one width and
drops LatentMoE. That same constraint blocks the faithful hero shape at EP64, blocks the matched
comparison from being matched, and blocks both architectures in #8236.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖

## 2026-08-14 — First EP64 measurements, and the compile wall behind them

Two one-rack runs logged throughput before finishing. Sixty-four GB200s, sixteen nodes, one
process per GPU, fabric transport, two layers, sixty-four experts (one per rank), three steps.

| run | MFU final / p50 / mean | tokens/s | drop fraction | MFU samples |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `mok-ep64-056-validate` | 13.10% / 9.28% / 8.26% | 2,190,297 | 18.84% | 4 |
| `mok-ep64-055-validate` | 12.89% / 7.75% / 7.32% | 2,156,589 | 18.10% | 4 |

Against the 26.2835% MFU / 309,091 tok/s / 7.228% drop reference, read carefully:

- **MFU is about half the reference** and is the number that matters. On the question the work
  exists to answer, this configuration does not clear the bar.
- **Throughput is not comparable.** Two layers against the hero's forty-eight means roughly
  twenty-four times less compute per token, so 2.19M tok/s is a depth artifact rather than a win.
- **Drops are worse, not better**: 18.8% here against 7.228%, and against 0% at EP4. Sixty-four
  experts over sixty-four ranks leaves one expert per rank, so routing imbalance hits the model's
  1.1 capacity factor far harder than two experts per rank did.
- **Four samples over three steps.** Mean (8.26%) sits well below final (13.10%), which is a run
  still climbing out of warmup. Treat these as an order of magnitude, not a measurement.

### Why there is nothing at greater depth

Every other one-rack attempt died in XLA compilation without reaching a step, so none of them
logged anything.

| configuration | outcome |
| --- | --- |
| sharded autotuning on | compile deadlock, every rank at zero CPU in `backend_compile_and_load` |
| sharded autotuning off, 4 layers, 1 slot | killed at fifteen minutes, still compiling |
| sharded autotuning off, 4 layers, 2 slots | SIGABRT at the fifty-minute timeout, still compiling |
| same, ninety-minute timeout | over two hours, no step |
| `--xla_gpu_autotune_level=1` | seventy-eight minutes, no step |
| 48 layers, 192 experts | `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED: 147.83GiB` inside `jit_train_step` |

Autotune level changed nothing, so the cost is not the autotune search. It is XLA compiling a
sixty-four-way SPMD module, upstream of anything in this branch: the megakernel and the fabric
transport are both proven at sixty-four ranks, and the reservation protocol was verified there --
all sixty-four agreeing on generations 2/4/6/8 forward and 10/12/14/16 backward.

The persistent compilation cache only records a compile that finishes, so none of the killed runs
left anything behind for the next one. Changing `--num-steps` alone also misses the cache, since
the schedule is baked into the graph.

### What this means

EP64 iteration is impractical until the compile cost is addressed or a cache is warmed for the
target shape, and that blocks the EP arm as much as this one. The matched baseline is still
missing: the one-node EP arm measured 2.37% MFU against its own 26.2835% reference, so it cannot
serve as a comparison.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖

## 2026-08-14 — Correction: the compile wall follows expert count, not rank count

The previous update attributed the one-rack compile cost to XLA lowering a sixty-four-way SPMD
module and suggested taking it up as an EP64 problem. That was wrong, and the correction matters
because it moves the investigation off a rack and onto one node.

A single node with 192 experts hits the same wall: four GPUs, four layers, twenty-eight minutes of
`backend_compile_and_load` and still going at the timeout. Rank count was not the variable.

| configuration | local experts x layers | compiled |
| --- | --- | --- |
| EP4, 8 experts, 48 layers | 2 x 48 | yes -- the 24.41% MFU run |
| EP64, 64 experts, 2 layers | 1 x 2 | yes -- the 13.10% MFU run |
| EP64, 64 experts, 4 layers | 1 x 4 | no, over two hours |
| EP64, 192 experts, 2 layers | 3 x 2 | no, over seventy-six minutes |
| EP4, 192 experts, 4 layers | 48 x 4 | no, over twenty-eight minutes on four GPUs |

Every configuration that ever produced a step carries the MoE structure that the matched comparison
already pins to eight experts. That pin now looks less like a modelling choice and more like the
only shape that compiles.

Two consequences.

The open questions about competitiveness are blocked on this rather than on anything in the branch.
The EP64 MFU of 13.10% is measured at two layers, the worst compute-to-communication ratio, so it
is a floor; the 18.84% drop rate is measured at sixty-four experts, one per rank, against a
reference that runs 192. Both need configurations that do not currently compile, and the attempt to
settle the drop rate on one node -- where parallelism is irrelevant to the answer, since drops are
routing against per-expert capacity -- failed the same way.

It is reproducible in under half an hour on four GPUs, and it blocks the ragged-a2a arm identically.
That makes it far cheaper to chase than the rack runs it has been costing.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖

## 2026-08-14 — Correcting the previous comment: both rank count and expert count matter

The comment above claimed the compile wall follows expert count and not rank count. The table in
that same comment contradicts it, and the claim should not stand.

- EP4, 8 experts, 48 layers -- two local experts across forty-eight layers -- compiles.
- EP64, 64 experts, 4 layers -- one local expert across four layers -- does not, at over two hours.

The second is far smaller by the "local experts times layers" measure I proposed, yet it is the one
that fails. Rank count is doing real work here. What the earlier comment got right is that expert
count also matters independently: EP4 with 192 experts, forty-eight local per rank, fails at four
layers on a single node.

So both dimensions contribute and neither alone accounts for the data. The one thing that is
directly supported is narrower and still useful: at sixty-four ranks, going from two layers to four
moves compile from roughly ten minutes to over two hours, which is a superlinearity in depth that
does not appear at four ranks. Anyone chasing this should treat rank count and per-rank expert count
as separate axes and measure the surface rather than assume a product.

The single-node reproduction stands and is still the cheap way in: four GPUs, 192 experts, four
layers, twenty-eight minutes and unfinished.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖

## 2026-08-15 — EP64 trains dropless on one rack; retracting the drop and compile-wall reports

Three earlier comments here are wrong and are withdrawn: the 18.84% drop reading, the claim that a
compile wall follows expert count, and its follow-up saying both rank and expert count matter.
There is no compile wall. The drop rate was a transient sampled at its worst step.

### One rack, sixteen layers, sixty-four experts, twenty-five updates

`mok-ep64-151-gate` completed, absorbing two preemptions and a coordinator restart.

| steps >= 15 | value |
| --- | --- |
| MFU mean / median / final | 18.80% / 19.28% / 21.87% |
| tokens/s (raw, 16 layers) | 686,690 mean, 798,551 final |
| tokens/s (normalised to 48 layers) | ~229,000 mean, ~266,000 final |
| drop fraction | zero from step 17 onward |

Read the normalised column, not the raw one. Sixteen layers is a third of the hero depth, so raw
tokens/s carries a factor of three that has nothing to do with the backend. Normalised, it sits
alongside the sealed v15 two-rack run's 276,982 tokens/s per rack, and the MFU figures agree too:
21.87% here against that run's 20.25%. MFU is the depth-normalised metric and the honest
comparison, and against the 26.2835% reference this is roughly 83%, not an improvement.

The result that does stand is the drop rate: zero from step 17, against the reference's 7.228%.

### The drop rate was never a property of the configuration

Drop fraction tracks routing entropy almost exactly. The router leaves initialisation near the
uniform bound of `ln 64 = 4.159`, dips, and recovers; drops peak with the dip and vanish as it
closes.

| step | 2 | 4 | 8 | 12 | 17 | 24 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| drop fraction | 0.318 | 0.135 | 0.026 | 0.003 | 0 | 0 |
| routing entropy | 3.020 | 3.570 | 3.943 | 4.008 | 4.113 | 4.152 |

The 18.84% previously reported here was step two of a three-step run: the trough. Upstream MoK is
dropless by construction and traps on overflow, so every drop in this backend comes from
`build_schedule` clipping to a static capacity, and that capacity's factor is exactly the
peak-to-mean expert load it absorbs. Two tests now pin that contract, and a CPU probe reproduces
the behaviour at any rank count without GPUs.

### There is no compile wall

The earlier comments attributed long pre-step stalls to XLA compilation scaling with expert count.
A `py-spy` dump of a stalled rank shows `pxla.py __call__`, which is `ExecuteReplicated` -- the
ranks are executing, not compiling. Disabling XLA autotuning outright changed nothing, which is
consistent. Expert count, depth, memory, autotune duplication and the megakernel build were each
tested and each ruled out; a single process reaches 48 layers and 64 experts without trouble.

Two unrelated faults were producing those stalls.

The first is an intermittent device-side deadlock in the cross-process fabric path: all GPUs pinned
at full utilisation, ranks spinning in `WaitCompletionKernel`, no progress. It reproduces at
roughly 29% on four processes and more often on eight, correlates with cluster contention, and is
**unfixed**. An `atomicMax` change to the peer-visible progress cells was tried and reverted: it
corrects a real latent bug -- a cell read with `>=` should not be written by unconditional exchange
-- but made no difference to the hang across a matched A/B.

The second is preemption. `promoted_dropless_v12` sets zero preemption retries, zero failure
retries and zero tolerated task failures, which is right for a seal and fatal for iteration: a rack
run pays twenty minutes of compile before its first update, so one preemption discards the attempt.
That, not the backend, is why this gate had no measurement. `launch_mok_like` now takes
`--max-retries-preemption`, `--max-retries-failure` and `--max-task-failures`.

### Still open

Forty-eight layers at EP64 does not fit: rematerialization reports 240.81 GiB against a 158.13 GiB
budget. Raising the memory fraction or lowering the capacity factor does not close that.

Two racks has not reached a first step across roughly eight attempts. Every failure is the JAX
coordination service becoming unreachable during distributed init, which fans out to 128 processes
at that size. It is a distributed-init scaling problem rather than a backend one and wants its own
investigation.

The proposed 8/384 architecture cannot be expressed. Both it and the current production shape are
latent MoE, and the backend rejects `latent_dim`. The kernel itself keeps the routed and shared
paths separate throughout and our FFI performs the shared-plus-routed sum, so the change is bounded:
two widths through the FFI, one `hidden_dim_col_blocks` split in the backward task decomposition,
and moving that sum into JAX so the routed result can be expanded first.

issues.author: dlwh
issues.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

No CODA RMS-GatedNorm candidate met the EP64 production gate. The final tuned treatment completed a concurrent 25-step A/B on 64 GB200 GPUs and improved throughput by 0.478% by ratio of medians, below the 0.78% placement floor, while adding 7.344 GiB peak HBM. Reducing `NCCL_BUFFSIZE` from 1 MiB to 256 KiB validated Matt's scratch-memory diagnosis and let the integrated treatment train, but the margin was too small and one gradient stayed outside the strict numerical gate. The conclusion is to keep #8153 as a research record and not extract a production branch.

### Helpful links
- [Final logbook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/grug-coda-rms-backward/.agents/logbooks/grug-moe-coda-rms.md)
- [Research PR](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8153)
- Final tuned EP64 W&B: [XLA](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/pr8153-ep-integrated-forward-tuned-nccl256k-ab-v1-xla-20260814), [treatment](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/pr8153-ep-integrated-forward-tuned-nccl256k-ab-v1-quack-coda-20260814)
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Goal

Apply CODA's producer-epilogue idea to the Grug RMS-GatedNorm boundary and exceed the measured 0.78% placement floor at the production EP64 hero shape without unacceptable loss drift or memory growth.

## Final EP64 result

Both arms ran concurrently, started on their first attempts, completed 25 steps, and used identical `NCCL_BUFFSIZE=262144` settings. Scores use steps 5-24.

| Metric | XLA | Tuned fused treatment | Change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Step duration | 17.017147 s | 16.936176 s | -0.476% |
| Throughput | 246,475.161 tok/s | 247,653.925 tok/s | +0.478% |
| MFU | 23.01408% | 23.12415% | +0.110 pp |
| Peak HBM | 174.221 GiB | 181.565 GiB | +7.344 GiB |

Same-step paired throughput improved 0.642%; strict timestamp-overlap paired throughput improved 0.364%. Both are below the promotion floor. Loss moved from 11.79909 to 5.99930 for XLA and from 11.79906 to 6.01493 for the treatment.

Four-device numerical checks passed the 1.0% scaled-error gate for output, input, norm gain, and down-projection weight gradients. The up-projection weight gradient remained finite but measured 1.149%, inside the 1.25% diagnostic band and outside the strict gate.

## What worked

- Keeping GatedNorm reverse in XLA and fusing only RMS reverse reduced peak HBM by 2.94 GiB, but throughput fell 0.28%.
- Fusing the delayed down projection and gated output removed full normalized/gate forward intermediates.
- `NCCL_BUFFSIZE=262144` provided enough staging headroom for the integrated treatment to complete EP64 training.
- Exact-shape launch tuning reduced the two forward kernels' projected combined latency by 1.63% with unchanged component parity.

## Negative results

- Split fused reverse: 2.36% slower and 4.92 GiB more HBM.
- Fused down-weight gradient: 3.09% slower, 4.29 GiB more HBM, and loss divergence after step 19.
- RMS-only reverse: 0.28% slower despite a 2.94 GiB HBM reduction.
- Integrated forward with a 1 MiB NCCL buffer: deterministic first-step AllToAll OOM at 184.29 GiB.
- Integrated forward with a 256 KiB NCCL buffer: fit and remained numerically stable, but the untuned and tuned A/B gains were 0.757% and 0.478%, respectively.

## Links

- [Full experiment branch](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/codex/grug-coda-rms-backward)
- [Final logbook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/grug-coda-rms-backward/.agents/logbooks/grug-moe-coda-rms.md)
- [Earlier logbook snapshot](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/e6f67c0484/.agents/logbooks/grug-moe-coda-rms.md)
- Final tuned EP64 W&B: [XLA](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/pr8153-ep-integrated-forward-tuned-nccl256k-ab-v1-xla-20260814), [treatment](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/pr8153-ep-integrated-forward-tuned-nccl256k-ab-v1-quack-coda-20260814)
- Untuned integrated EP64 W&B: [XLA](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/pr8153-ep-integrated-delayed-output-nccl256k-ab-v1-xla-20260814), [treatment](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/pr8153-ep-integrated-delayed-output-nccl256k-ab-v1-quack-coda-20260814)
- RMS-only EP64 W&B: [XLA](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/pr8153-ep-rms-only-nccl1m-ab-v1-xla-20260814), [treatment](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/pr8153-ep-rms-only-nccl1m-ab-v1-quack-coda-20260814)
- Research PR: #8153

## Conclusion

The memory-fit workaround is valid for this exact EP64 treatment, but the final implementation does not justify production extraction. The measured throughput gain is below the placement floor, peak HBM is higher, and one gradient remains outside the strict numerical gate. #8153 should remain a research record rather than merge as a production optimization.

issues.body:
MarinSkyRL [#284](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/284) consolidated SkyRL into one root distribution and frozen lock. [#296](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/296) now installs that distribution from exact commit `7746fe66ee94accbd382f2b64467950a0956ec59` and a named profile inside the cluster-configured standard Iris task image. Marin [#7883](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/7883) identifies an RL artifact with the same commit and profile.

The maintained image-free paths are live. [Marin vLLM `marin-vllm-gpu-20260805-fa50698a9a30`](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/releases/tag/marin-vllm-gpu-20260805-fa50698a9a30) publishes immutable H100/x86_64 and GB200/aarch64 wheels with the main extension, cuMem allocator, Grug registry support, and source provenance. The frozen environment passed a 30-step dense Qwen3-0.6B FSDP gate on H100 and a Grug rollout-to-FSDP2 checkpoint/resume gate on GB200 in [MarinSkyRL Actions](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/actions/runs/31041073109). Torch, CUDA user-space libraries, Ray, FSDP, and the remaining Python dependencies resolve from the lock. These routes need neither a SkyRL image nor a private wheelhouse.

Remaining work:

- Add bounded x86_64 and aarch64 Megatron live gates from the same frozen environment before declaring maintained Megatron configurations image-free.
- Publish a `flash-attn` wheel compatible with the locked Torch/CUDA ABI for maintained policy configurations that set `trainer.flash_attn=true`. Eager policy training and Marin vLLM rollout do not require it.
- Package the opt-in GDN `fla_tilelang` overlay if that backend remains maintained.
- Move the standalone checkpoint-reshard and CoreWeave monitor entry points to the frozen bootstrap, then delete the legacy GPU-RL path module, Dockerfiles, build scripts, tests, and image-build guidance.
- Record the resolved lock identity, architecture, standard task-image digest, and exceptional wheel hashes in terminal provenance.

DeepGEMM is not required by the maintained BF16 dense or Grug routes; those routes disable it. Add a compatible plugin only if a maintained configuration selects it.

Done when every maintained launcher and utility installs a frozen root profile in the standard Iris task image, the remaining live matrix passes, and no maintained entry point imports a legacy image path.

The [packaging design](https://loom.rjp.io/s/rkdrs7y2/artifacts/marinskyrl-packaging-migration) records the execution boundary.

comments.author: weaverbot
comments.body:
🤖 Surfaced by the harbor unification/catch-up ([marin-community/harbor#73](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/pull/73), which folds the standalone `harbor_config` package into `harbor.models` and retires the config-wheel publisher): MarinSkyRL is a downstream consumer of the harbor fork that this affects, and it manages that dependency less safely than Marin does.

Today MarinSkyRL depends on `harbor[analysis,datasets,daytona]` (terminal-bench RL environments) plus the standalone `harbor-config` wheel, and its `[tool.uv.sources] harbor = { git = … }` floats to `main` (the lock just captured `24e5e67a`). So once the harbor catch-up lands, any unrelated MarinSkyRL relock silently pulls the folded harbor and breaks the `harbor-config` wheel dependency.

Proposed follow-up scope — fold into this issue or split, your call:
- Pin harbor to an explicit immutable ref instead of floating `main`, so it only moves on an intentional bump (`flash-attn`/`harbor-config` are already release-pinned; `harbor` is the one floating git source).
- Give MarinSkyRL a Marin-style `update-external` plus one declared e2e (a bounded terminal-bench rollout through Harbor) so a harbor bump is deliberate and validated — the SkyRL analogue of Marin's `config/external/harbor` + `aime-smoke`.
- Migrate off the standalone `harbor-config` wheel to `harbor.models` (the `_harbor_compat.py` shim already covers the orchestrator API; this is the packaging axis). First exercise of the new model.

Not proposing harbor+skyrl lockstep every week — that would make the weekly harbor ferry hostage to SkyRL's RL validation. Keep them decoupled and record the coordination requirement in the harbor `migration.toml` (done in the harbor pin PR) so a breaking harbor change flags a coordinated SkyRL migration instead of drifting in silently.

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
After Harbor applies the agent network policy to a running Daytona sandbox, a new TCP connection to the probe host sometimes still succeeds. In a 1600-trial TMax pilot (Qwen3.6-27B, terminus-2, Daytona EVAL org, 64 concurrent trials), 9 trials (0.56%) failed with `NetworkLockdownError: pypi.org:443 is still reachable after the agent network policy`. All 9 failed closed: the trial stopped before the agent started, so no agent ran with open egress. Each failed trial is lost and has to be run again.

The policy is a domain allow-list containing only `iris.oa.dev`. Harbor calls `DaytonaMachine.update_network` ([machine.py:298](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f07e07ac26ef2457f98cb7a7adfa7e96e9c031a0/lib/shellbox/src/shellbox/backends/daytona/machine.py#L298)), which awaits `sandbox.update_network_settings`. It then probes `timeout 10 bash -c 'exec 3<>/dev/tcp/pypi.org/443'` ([daytona.py:285-300](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f07e07ac26ef2457f98cb7a7adfa7e96e9c031a0/vendor/harbor/src/harbor/environments/daytona.py#L285-L300)). A probe exit code of 0 raises the error. Both code paths are on the pilot branch `task/qwen36-tmax-pilot`, not on main.

Reproduce:
1. Start a Daytona sandbox with an unrestricted network policy.
2. Call `update_network` with `DaytonaNetworkPolicy(DOMAIN_ALLOW_LIST, "iris.oa.dev")`.
3. Immediately open a TCP connection to `pypi.org:443`. About 1 in 180 sandboxes accepts it.

Expected: once `update_network_settings` returns, the policy is in force, or the API gives a way to wait until it is.

Failed trials (finish times 2026-11-14 UTC):

| Trial | Finished |
|---|---|
| task_007905_85674759__Z6SBrB3 | 03:48:57 |
| task_005909_4d8203db__rEaeamb | 04:00:05 |

| task_005979_2298ae0c__FfAiEVf | 05:12:22 |
| task_006347_d2193fb9__ueDxzAA | 05:12:55 |

Observations:
- **The failures are spread over the run, not clustered.**
- **They don't repeat on the same task.** No task failed this way twice. Task 006798's second attempt hit a different error, an apply failure.
- **The cause is unknown.** It may be a propagation delay after `update_network_settings` returns (inferred, not confirmed).
- **One-sandbox smoke checks passed every time.** In them, a held connection and new connections were all blocked after the update (`experiments/post_training/tmax_reserve/lockdown_smoke.py` on the same branch).
- **The rest of the run's lockdowns held.** 4 other trials failed to apply the policy at all, each with `DaytonaConnectionError: Failed to update network settings: [Errno 104] Connection reset by peer`. That is a transient API failure that retries would cover.
- **No apt traffic reached the mirror** in any of the 1600 trials.

# Research

On `task/qwen36-tmax-pilot`, Harbor waits for Daytona's network update and treats one successful `/dev/tcp/pypi.org/443` connect as a lockdown failure; the nine errors establish only that this TCP connect returned zero. [Daytona's network documentation](https://www.daytona.io/docs/en/network-limits/#https-traffic) says its domain allow list enforces HTTPS by host name through an egress proxy, so the TCP result alone does not establish that an HTTPS request reached PyPI. The smoke test waits 20 seconds after the update before probing; it cannot distinguish TCP-only success from update propagation delay. I found no overlapping open PR.

- [machine.py](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f07e07ac26ef2457f98cb7a7adfa7e96e9c031a0/lib/shellbox/src/shellbox/backends/daytona/machine.py#L298-L300) — awaits the SDK update

# Proposed Fix

1. Reproduce at the pilot's 64-concurrent-sandbox setting. Record the update-return time, immediate and repeated TCP results, a request for recognizable PyPI content, an allow-listed `iris.oa.dev` control request, and sandbox IDs. Keep agents stopped during diagnostics; classify proxy denial, upstream content, and inconclusive requests separately.
2. If TCP succeeds while the proxy denies HTTPS, replace the TCP-only gate with a probe that recognizes the denial and fails closed on inconclusive results. Add a behavioral regression test.
3. If PyPI content is reachable after the update, measure how long it remains reachable, report sandbox IDs and timestamps to Daytona, and add a bounded verification wait that never starts the agent while the probe is reachable or inconclusive.
4. Validate on a comparable 64-concurrent cohort with enough updates to compare against the pilot's 9/1600 failures. Report the observed failure rate and any confirmed disallowed HTTPS responses.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
Native SFTSpec Snowball d1024 training on one 8×H100 node passes forward evaluation but can hang in the first optimizer update. Every GPU reports 100% utilization, zero memory traffic and roughly 120–215W; Python rank main threads remain in XLA ExecuteReplicated. No completed update appears after more than five minutes. This blocks unmodified-runtime loss curves and throughput comparisons. d768 full-target training also stalled; d768 assistant-target and both d512 masks completed 20 updates.

Reproduce:
1. Load `open-athena/Snowflake-d1024-Base-262K-2026.10.19` at revision `dd3c5e3c156cfbe936fc0b59932c747e47c21d04` through native SFTSpec→TrainLmConfig→train_lm. Use sequence length 262144, global batch 8, microbatch 1, context parallel 4/data parallel 2, expert parallel 1, FP32 master parameters, BF16 computation, Sonic dispatch, gpu_fa4_cute attention, offloaded Muon-H optimizer and cuda_async allocator. The raw HF checkpoint evaluation and a second evaluation after resetting seven output-head token columns to fixed anchor columns both finish and match independently computed losses within 0.001. Training controls use assistant-only targets, data/trainer seed 0, sequential 262144-position packing and the pinned phase 0 Experiment 1 mixture. Its complete component paths, weights, reserved split and shuffle settings are in the consumed-config receipt linked below.
2. Use `XLA_FLAGS="--xla_gpu_shard_autotuning=false --xla_gpu_nccl_termination_timeout_seconds=600"` and execute the first backward/update. The local reproduction entry point is `experiments/post_training/snowball_isoflop/diagnostic.py`; source 33b69d10df preserves the isolated controls and later 97f6a242e6 exposes the explicit SFTSpec runtime field. These commits are local research commits, currently unpublished.
3. Compare the controls below, each starting from the same two-flag baseline in step 2. Baseline command-buffer and async-collective behavior is left at the JAX runtime default; neither has an extra override. Read-only inspection of a fresh campaign worker confirms jax, jaxlib, jax-cuda13-plugin and jax-cuda13-pjrt all 0.11.1. These match the GPU dependency pins used by the diagnostic source.

Expected: the first optimizer update completes, followed by finite training steps, without forced host launch synchronization.

| Runtime control | Observed result |
|---|---|
| Source async-collective runtime | First-update stall |
| Add `--xla_gpu_disable_async_collectives=ALLCOLLECTIVES` | First-update stall; NCCL collective counts agree across all ranks (AllGather 1460, ReduceScatter 99, AllReduce 46 globally) |
| Add only `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1` | First-update stall |
| Add only `--xla_gpu_enable_command_buffer=` | First-update stall |
| Both command buffers off and `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1` | 20 finite updates, permanent step 19 checkpoint, both initial-loss gates pass |
| Source runtime under Nsight Systems CUDA/NVTX tracing | 14 finite updates before deliberate bounded termination; CUDA graphs remain active |

The successful unprofiled joint control's first update took about 99 seconds; subsequent warm inclusive median 9.2473s/update, minimum unused allocator capacity 55.54% (the JAX allocator is limited to approximately 75% of physical GPU memory). One profiled run progressed while the unprofiled source-runtime attempt stalled; repeatability of this difference is not established. Its available trace contains 1,531,280 kernels across all 8 GPUs and 91,112 cuGraphLaunch calls. The report emitted a StringStorage processing warning, so exported events have that caveat. Successful completed kernels do not identify the operation stuck in unprofiled execution. NCCL 2.31.2, CUDA runtime 13.3, driver API 13.2 were reported. Agreement of NCCL counters in the synchronous-collective control does not prove which kernel or communication operation is responsible.

Preserved profile: `s3://marin-us-east-08a/marin/users/benfeuer/snowball-isoflop/2026.11.13.9/diagnostic-kernel-profile-d1024-assistant-seed0-n20/nsys/r00000-gb95de0.nsys-rep` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-08a%2Fmarin%2Fusers%2Fbenfeuer%2Fsnowball-isoflop%2F2026.11.13.9%2Fdiagnostic-kernel-profile-d1024-assistant-seed0-n20%2Fnsys%2Fr00000-gb95de0.nsys-rep)); exported summary is `analysis/kernel-summary.json` beside its nsys directory. Control directories in that same 2026.11.13.9 prefix are `calibration-d1024-assistant-seed0-n20` (source runtime), `diagnostic-serial-collectives-d1024-assistant-seed0-n20`, `diagnostic-launch-blocking-d1024-assistant-seed0-n20`, `diagnostic-no-command-buffer-d1024-assistant-seed0-n20`, and `diagnostic-synchronous-launches-d1024-assistant-seed0-n20`. Each preserves `consumed-config.json`, `dispatch.json` and initial-evaluation receipts. The complete successful joint-control config is [available in Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-08a%2Fmarin%2Fusers%2Fbenfeuer%2Fsnowball-isoflop%2F2026.11.13.9%2Fdiagnostic-synchronous-launches-d1024-assistant-seed0-n20%2Fconsumed-config.json). Config and profile access require Marin credentials; the local source commits are not yet a public standalone reproducer.

Exact isolated-control entry point, from the research checkout inside an 8-GPU Iris coordinator: `python -m experiments.post_training.snowball_isoflop.diagnostic --size 1024 --mask assistant --runtime synchronous-launches --h100-hour-limit 3 --run`. Replace the runtime value with `serial-collectives`, `launch-blocking` or `no-command-buffer` for the other controls. The coordinator must target cw-rno2a with interactive priority and 259200-second timeout.

Related investigations: #7110 (concurrent TVM-FFI invocation), #8870 (multi-rack ragged EP hang). This single-node CP4/data2 Sonic case has not been reduced to either mechanism.

Fresh six-cell calibration update (2026-11-14 02:51UTC): both d1024 masks with the joint runtime progressed beyond15 finite updates. All four source-runtime arms (d512 full/assistant and d768 full/assistant) passed both initial-loss gates but stalled in their first update for more than five minutes. Read-only samples of each rank main thread show ExecuteReplicated; all32GPUs report100% utilization, zero memory traffic and117–171W. The successful V9 d512/d768 assistant trajectories and these V10 stalls show that earlier small-size successes do not establish reliable source-runtime execution. The newer source adds token-count metric reductions relative to the original calibration; this is an attribution caveat, although CPU comparison verifies unchanged numerical training settings. All source-runtime failed-arm receipts remain under `2026.11.13.10/calibration-d{512,768}-{full,assistant}-seed0-n20/`; their scoped recovery uses separate `calibration-recovery-` identities.

Runtime-control update (2026-11-14 04:25UTC): command buffers off plus launch blocking completed20-update native calibrations for d768 full and both d1024 masks, but still stalled both d512 masks and d768 assistant. Adding `--xla_gpu_disable_async_collectives=ALLCOLLECTIVES` to that joint setting completed20 finite updates for BOTH d512 masks and BOTH d768 masks, with dual initial-loss gates, finished trackers, permanent step19 checkpoints and safe allocator headroom. These are scoped loss-curve workarounds; their timings are excluded from source-runtime throughput comparisons. The corresponding SFTSpec runtime implementation is in local research source3a38e030d0 (unpublished).

A source-runtime d1024 `ring_gather_combine` control at CP4/data2 also stalled at the first update. A late CUDA-GDB attachment timed out before kernel queries; the job later failed, so retain an intervention caveat and do not infer a particular blocked kernel. Its archived output is preserved at `s3://marin-us-east-08a/marin/users/benfeuer/snowball-isoflop/2026.11.13.10/diagnostic-ring-r2/debugger-outputs.tar.zst` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-08a%2Fmarin%2Fusers%2Fbenfeuer%2Fsnowball-isoflop%2F2026.11.13.10%2Fdiagnostic-ring-r2%2Fdebugger-outputs.tar.zst)).

A d512 assistant CP8/data1/Sonic/offload-true control using SOURCE runtime (neither extra compiler flags nor launch blocking) completed20 finite updates, both gates, permanent step19 and zero measured sender/receiver drops. Minimum allocator headroom80.19%; warm inclusive71,600 positions/s/GPU. Its supervisor recorded a rank0 cleanup segfault, although job, tracker and native checkpoint gates passed. All compared layout diagnostics use dispatch-count instrumentation, which differs from the main calibration and remains an attribution caveat. CP4/data2 offload-false was interrupted before training, so it does not establish an offload result. Geometry is a useful discriminator; a causal kernel mechanism remains unproven.

Batch-probe update (2026-11-14 04:35UTC): original SOURCE runtime also stalls d512, d768 and d1024 assistant-target CP4/data2/Sonic/offload-true probes at global batch2, microbatch1, accumulation1. All three pass both initial gates; none records an update more than9 minutes after the first batch is loaded. Read-only snapshots show all24GPUs at100% utilization and0% memory utilization, approximately118–217W. d512/d1024 main threads remain in ExecuteReplicated; d768 waits on ArrayImpl._value while reading the resulting loss scalar. Each stalled probe was stopped; total allocation6.64272H100-hours. These cells provide no valid throughput or batch-saturation measurements. Exact receipts are under `2026.11.13.10/B-accumulation-cp4-dp2-ep1-r1-sonic-offload1-mb1-acc1-grug_moe_muonh_v1-lr5e-05-d{512,768,1024}-assistant-seed0-n8/` beside the previous artifacts. This extends the observed failure beyond accumulation4/globalbatch8, without proving its cause.

The d1024 full-mask three-setting runtime (joint setting plus ALLCOLLECTIVES) also completed20 finite updates, both initial gates, finished tracking and a permanent step19 checkpoint. The matching assistant confirmation is running; uniform loss-phase runtime has not yet been selected from that pending result.

CP8 feasibility update (2026-11-14 04:59UTC): source-runtime batch8/microbatch1/accumulation8/Sonic/offload-true probes completed8 finite updates for d512 AND d768. Both have finished trackers, dual initial-loss gates, permanent step7 checkpoints and zero measured sender/receiver drops. Warm inclusive positions/s/GPU are48,324 and48,514; minimum allocator headroom81.20% and73.08%. Both supervisors killed rank0 during cleanup despite successful job/tracker/checkpoint gates. The d1024 CP8 cell passed both initial gates but stalled before its first update; two read-only samples several minutes apart show ExecuteReplicated and all8GPUs100% utilization/0% memory utilization/~118–130W. It was stopped after both smaller endpoints were verified. Thus CP8 is a positive discriminator for two sizes, not a universal recovery. All three use identical dispatch-count instrumentation and the original two E2 flags; no loss-phase runtime overrides.

The three-setting d1024 assistant confirmation also completed its first update and reached final native checkpoint/export, but its3-H100-hour bound interrupted export with only19 published training rows. It is not accepted as completed calibration and is not another first-update stall. A separate fresh4-hour confirmation preserves the interrupted artifacts and the full calibration requirements.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖

# Research

The compiled training step computes gradients and applies the optimizer in one execution. The reported forward evaluations and runtime controls do not identify which operation stalls. Command buffers disabled together with `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1` completed 20 updates; each control alone stalled. One source-runtime run under Nsight reached 14 updates, but repeatability is unknown. The cited diagnostic commits `33b69d10df` and `97f6a242e6` are absent from this checkout and GitHub; the exact workload cannot yet be reproduced from published source. [#7110](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7110) and [#8870](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8870) involve different kernels or topologies and do not identify this stall.

**Relevant code**
- [`trainer.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/levanter/src/levanter/trainer.py#L726-L749) — gradients and optimizer share a compiled step.
- [`snowball.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/levanter/src/levanter/models/snowball.py#L430-L455) — Snowball attention dispatch.
- [`_fa4_cute.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_fa4_cute.py#L311-L335) — H100 attention backend.
- [`sonic.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/sonic.py#L248-L310) — Sonic dispatch and backward.
- [`muonh.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/levanter/src/levanter/optim/muonh.py#L54-L100) — Muon-H optimizer construction.

# Proposed Fix

1. Publish the isolated `diagnostic.py`, its SFTSpec runtime field, and exact dependency pins in a reviewable branch. Link its consumed-config receipt. Give every trial a first-update deadline and preserve its result and source revision.
2. On the same 8×H100 configuration, repeat the source runtime and passing joint control three times each. Run a separate traced source-runtime arm to measure the Nsight effect. Record per-rank progress, NCCL RAS, XLA executable dumps, and loaded CUDA/NCCL versions; stop each stalled trial after a 10-minute first-update deadline.
3. Split the first update at the gradient/optimizer boundary with the same parameters, batch, and mesh: evaluate gradients without applying them, then apply the optimizer to captured gradients. If gradients stall, replace FA4 and Sonic independently. Capture a GPU kernel/stream stack from a stalled rank before changing more runtime flags. These ablations localize a suspect; they do not by themselves prove a cause if recompilation changes launch order.
4. Fix the identified component in Marin or report a minimal reproducer upstream. Validate the original unprofiled runtime without launch synchronization across three cold 20-update runs, with finite losses, the existing initial-loss gates, and warm-step timing against the 9.2473 s joint-control median. Add a regression test for the isolated failure before opening a fix PR.

Source pin: `0a4a1a6eab6ce979d67e1337b322eea3f1f83acd`. Recipe: Exp1 + per-group clip 1, BF16 stored, adam_lr 1:1; stage 0 only, offloaded optimizer state. The historical optimizer applies Muon-H to dense matrices, Adam to rank-4 expert banks and AdamH to output_proj.

All cases below already had command buffers disabled, shard autotuning disabled and the Iris autotune cache enabled.

| Case | LR | Runtime | Outcome |
|---|---:|---|---|
| r5b | 2e-5 | EAGER, autotune level 4 | One successful 25-update run. First execution 58.33 s; updates 2–5 mean 44.08 s. All 15 eval sets completed at updates 15 and 25 (token-weighted NLL 0.672724 / 0.660441). |
| r6, two arms | 5e-5 / 1e-4 | EAGER, autotune level 4 | Both stalled in the first execution after compilation; stopped at the 900 s first-step rule. Zero completed updates. |
| r7, two arms | 5e-5 / 1e-4 | EAGER, autotune level 4, plus CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1 and ALLCOLLECTIVES | Both stalled in the first execution; stopped at the 600 s rule. Zero completed updates. |
| r5c | 2e-5 | LAZY, autotune level 0; no launch-blocking/ALLCOLLECTIVES overrides | Seven finite updates before deliberate cancellation. About 120 s/update; update-15 eval was not reached. |

The r6 deadline captures covered all 64 ranks per arm: 51 and 52 of 64, respectively, main stacks included `cuModuleLoadData → jax::cuda::TritonKernelCall`. In r7, all 64 captured main stacks in each arm instead included `cuLaunchKernelEx → ncclLaunchKernel → ncclGroupEnd → xla::gpu::NcclGroupLaunch`. Sampled GPUs showed 100% SM utilization and 0% memory utilization.

For each r7 arm, NCCL RAS samples at 07:00:49Z and 07:02:35Z on 2026-11-14 had **all 170 matched communicator/collective min/max counter entries unchanged**, with no communicators added or lost. Thus there was no observed counter advance over approximately 106 s.

The three-setting workaround reported here at 8 H100 has not qualified at our 64-H100/full-model geometry. The successful r5b run also did not establish reliability. LR constants differ across the successful and stalled cases, and the stack/counter observations do not identify a unique causal kernel. The level 0 result establishes several completed updates, not a completed held-out-eval qualification.

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
Worker-bound attempts in PREEMPTED state can retain `finished_at_ms = NULL` after their task retries as a newer attempt. Resource accounting continues charging the old attempt, but reconciliation excludes it. A full-slice TPU gang can then time out despite having enough lower-priority work to preempt.

This recurs after [issue 5918](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5918) and [PR 5920](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/5920). On 2026-11-12 around 23:54 UTC, controller SQL still showed six such attempt-0 rows on slice `t1v-n-8649f701`, on hosts 6, 33, 36, 37, 46 and 63. Every corresponding task had advanced to `current_attempt_id = 1`. Four newer attempts were running on a different slice; another was running on the same host; the remaining task had succeeded. The previously recorded ghost on `t1v-n-f0c8b705` was absent in this read. [Incident evidence](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/971) records the original evictions around 19:37 UTC and a subsequent INTERACTIVE 64-task gang that remained pending for an hour before scheduling timeout.

The controller's read-only GetProcessStatus response at 23:55 UTC reported base commit `260d937671`, tree hash `94088439c4`, and `dirty = false`. That revision contains these paths:

- [`preempt_one`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/260d937671/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/reconcile/task.py#L231) marks a worker-bound attempt PREEMPTED and rolls a retryable task back to PENDING. It deliberately leaves the attempt finish time unset until the worker confirms termination (`stamp_attempt_finished = row.current_worker_id is None`).
- [`commit_assignments`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/260d937671/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/ops/task.py#L100) increments the attempt ID, and [`assign_to_worker`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/260d937671/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/writes.py#L651) inserts the new attempt and advances the task's current attempt without finalizing the previous attempt.
- [`load_reconcile_rows`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/260d937671/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/reads.py#L1786) joins attempts to tasks on both task ID and `current_attempt_id = attempt_id`. Once attempt 1 exists, unfinished attempt 0 disappears from the reconcile plan. Observations outside that plan are filtered out.
- [`apply_one_transition`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/260d937671/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/reconcile/task.py#L333) also returns for a superseded attempt before the terminal-attempt backfill path.
- [`resource_usage_by_worker`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/260d937671/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/reads.py#L751) charges every worker-bound attempt with `finished_at_ms IS NULL`, including those older attempts.

[PR 7206](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/7206) changed preemption and placement to share a transaction and added dispatch gating while victims remain unfinished. It is relevant context, but this investigation does not establish that it introduced the leak. The current-attempt reconcile join dates to PR 6294. The unfinalized rows establish a persistent accounting leak; they do not prove whether the original processes are still alive.

Detect with the read-only controller query RPC:

```bash
uv run iris --cluster marin query -f csv "$(cat <<'SQL'
SELECT w.md_tpu_name, w.md_tpu_worker_id,
       a.task_id, a.attempt_id, a.state, a.finished_at_ms,
       t.current_attempt_id, t.state AS task_state,
       a.worker_id, t.current_worker_id
FROM task_attempts a
JOIN workers w ON w.worker_id = a.worker_id
JOIN tasks t ON t.task_id = a.task_id
WHERE a.worker_id IS NOT NULL
  AND a.finished_at_ms IS NULL
  AND a.state = 10
  AND a.attempt_id <> t.current_attempt_id
ORDER BY w.md_tpu_name, w.md_tpu_worker_id;
SQL
)"
```

Proposed fix: include superseded worker-bound unfinished attempts in reconciliation by removing the current-attempt condition from the join. When a superseded attempt receives a terminal observation, including the worker's MISSING outcome, backfill that attempt's finish time without changing the newer task or attempt. The planner must issue a stop or status probe for the old attempt according to its own terminal state, rather than copying the newer attempt's run intent. Preserve capacity reservation until termination is confirmed; eagerly stamping at preemption would release capacity while the old process may still be running.

Regression test: preempt a worker-bound task eligible for retry, assign attempt 1 before attempt 0's termination is observed, then report attempt 0 killed (and separately MISSING). Verify that the old attempt remains in the reconcile plan until confirmation, its finish time is stamped afterward, its resource charge disappears, and attempt 1's state is preserved. Exercise the gang case where a single leaked host prevents full-slice admission.

One-time recovery for existing rows belongs to Iris operators: after independently confirming that each selected old process is gone, operators can stamp `finished_at_ms` for an explicitly enumerated set of `(task_id, attempt_id, worker_id)` rows, guarded by `state = 10 AND finished_at_ms IS NULL` and a superseded-attempt check. Do not bulk-finalize all PREEMPTED rows: some may still own live processes. No cleanup or controller mutation was performed during this investigation.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

`load_reconcile_rows` drops an unfinished worker-bound attempt once `current_attempt_id` advances, while `resource_usage_by_worker` continues charging it. Restoring that row alone is insufficient: the worker planner currently derives intent from the newer task state, and `apply_one_transition` drops superseded-attempt observations before it can stamp the old finish time. No open PR overlaps this issue.

**Relevant code**
- [`reads.py#L1773`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/reads.py#L1773) — current-attempt reconcile join
- [`reads.py#L734`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/reads.py#L734) — unfinished-attempt resource charge
- [`worker.py#L129`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/reconcile/worker.py#L129) — worker intent selection
- [`task.py#L290`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/reconcile/task.py#L290) — superseded-attempt guard
- [`loader.py#L241`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/reconcile/loader.py#L241) — observation UID loads old attempts

# Proposed Fix

1. Join all unfinished worker-bound attempts to their task by task ID in the reconcile read, and carry whether each attempt is current in `ReconcileRow`.
2. Choose a superseded row's worker intent from its attempt state before considering the newer task state. Send a stop for a terminal old attempt (PREEMPTED uses `STOP_REASON_PREEMPTED`); probe a nonterminal old attempt without copying the newer attempt's run spec. Keep the preemption-victim dispatch gate active until the old attempt finishes.
3. On a terminal observation for a worker-bound, superseded attempt already in a terminal state, stamp only that attempt's `finished_at_ms`. Include the worker's MISSING outcome; leave the current task and newer attempt unchanged. Continue dropping nonterminal stale updates.
4. Add a regression that preempts attempt 0, assigns attempt 1 before termination is observed, and checks the reconcile plan and resource charge before and after KILLED and MISSING observations. Exercise full-slice gang admission with one occupied host. Run the Iris controller tests, repository lint, and PR review before landing. Existing rows require a separate operator recovery after process absence is verified.

issues.author: ravwojdyla-agent
issues.body:
Data Belay's intake (#11019) decides whether a Hugging Face dataset's license allows training on it. [`license_verdict`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ba30b94916cc174ad0b2786651f94c8e88e88235/experiments/data_belay/intake.py#L143) allows every license on the [Blue Oak Council list](https://blueoakcouncil.org/list) ([`BLUE_OAK_LICENSES_BY_RATING`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ba30b94916cc174ad0b2786651f94c8e88e88235/experiments/data_belay/intake.py#L29)) and OpenMDW. It rejects non-commercial and no-derivatives licenses, and sends `other`, `unknown` and every other id to a person. Datakit and dataset onboarding (the `add-dataset` skill) have no license check, and the allowlist lives in `experiments/data_belay/intake.py`, where they can't import it without depending on Data Belay.

Move the allowlist when Datakit or dataset onboarding needs a license check.

Done when:
- The allowlist and `license_verdict` live in a module that Data Belay and the second caller both import.
- The second caller checks licenses with it.
- Data Belay's intake tests pass unchanged.

issues.author: ravwojdyla-agent
issues.body:
Data Belay (#11019) judges a candidate dataset by the change in eval loss when a run trains on it, and it does not check the candidate's text for overlap with those evals. A candidate that holds eval questions or answers would read as a gain on that eval. The README lists this as a limit ([README](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ba30b94916cc174ad0b2786651f94c8e88e88235/experiments/data_belay/README.md#L317)).

Datakit already builds a Bloom filter over eval text ([`build_eval_bloom_step`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ba30b94916cc174ad0b2786651f94c8e88e88235/lib/marin/src/marin/datakit/decon.py#L1294), from the corpus that [`prepare_eval_corpus.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ba30b94916cc174ad0b2786651f94c8e88e88235/experiments/datakit/decontam/prepare_eval_corpus.py) stages) and flags documents with `decon_step` ([`decon_arm.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ba30b94916cc174ad0b2786651f94c8e88e88235/experiments/datakit/testbed/decon_arm.py)). That corpus covers the Artificial Analysis index benchmarks and the lm-eval tasks in `experiments/evals/task_configs.py`. Data Belay reads Paloma, Uncheatable Eval and the Eval Policy answer tasks (#10197), so the corpus may not cover all of them.

Done when:
- `data-belay prepare` reports the fraction of a candidate's prepared documents that the eval Bloom filter flags, for each eval group in the verdict.
- The eval corpus covers every eval set that the verdict reads, or the report names the ones it doesn't.
- The README's limit on contamination states what the scan covers.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖

# Research

Data Belay is still in [PR #11019](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11019); its `prepare` paths tokenize selected files with a document cap and write a cache manifest, but never scan those documents. Datakit's marker needs normalized text with document IDs and writes document flags plus a hash-to-eval index; its existing report computes exact totals but attributes only sampled examples. The open [#10541](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10541) → [#10836](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10836) → [#10938](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10938) stack adds required Uncheatable and Eval Policy coverage, but its v13 corpus is not staged yet; Paloma is absent from that corpus.

**Relevant code**
- [`prepare.py#L201-L223`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ba30b94916cc174ad0b2786651f94c8e88e88235/experiments/data_belay/prepare.py#L201-L223) — candidate cache inputs and manifest
- [`__main__.py#L209-L274`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ba30b94916cc174ad0b2786651f94c8e88e88235/experiments/data_belay/__main__.py#L209-L274) — both preparation routes
- [`judge.py#L63-L73`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ba30b94916cc174ad0b2786651f94c8e88e88235/experiments/data_belay/judge.py#L63-L73) — verdict groups
- [`decon.py#L802-L923`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/e9ae26899c90512195e68f0edec808bb42b88bf3/lib/marin/src/marin/datakit/decon.py#L802-L923) — reusable Bloom mark and flags
- [`paloma.py#L17-L45`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/e9ae26899c90512195e68f0edec808bb42b88bf3/experiments/datasets/paloma.py#L17-L45) — Paloma validation sources

# Proposed Fix

1. Build this as a follow-up to #11019 and the Datakit PR stack. Resolve the versioned Bloom in the candidate's region, validate its required manifests, and use the same 13-gram and item-match settings as the Datakit reference pipeline; fail preparation if the Bloom is unavailable.
2. Make `prepare` and `prepare-datakit` scan the exact raw documents their tokenized cache consumes, including the row cap, by feeding tokenization and Datakit marking from the same staged `id,text,partition_id` sample. Count each prepared document once in the denominator.
3. Join flagged documents' matched hashes to the Bloom's eval index, map eval IDs to the six verdict groups, and count each document once per group. Save counts, corpus version, scan settings, and task coverage with the cache manifest; print `flagged / prepared` for each covered group in `prepare` and `report`, and name any uncovered eval tasks instead of showing a zero rate. Audit revisions and splits of all verdict tasks against the corpus; Paloma needs a corpus entry from the existing in-region reconstructed text or an explicit uncovered label.
4. Test both preparation routes with a small real Parquet sample and Bloom: one document matching two groups, one clean document, a capped input, and an uncovered task. Check the persisted counts and report output without training runs.

issues.author: ravwojdyla-agent
issues.body:
Data Belay (#11019) scores each run's final checkpoint with its own multiple-choice scorer, [`experiments/data_belay/accuracy.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ba30b94916cc174ad0b2786651f94c8e88e88235/experiments/data_belay/accuracy.py#L120). Levanter has one already, [`LevanterHarnessLM`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ba30b94916cc174ad0b2786651f94c8e88e88235/lib/levanter/src/levanter/eval_harness.py#L457), and the two prompt some tasks differently:

- [`_hellaswag`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ba30b94916cc174ad0b2786651f94c8e88e88235/experiments/data_belay/accuracy.py#L94) skips lm-eval's `[title]` and bracket cleanup.
- [`_mmlu`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ba30b94916cc174ad0b2786651f94c8e88e88235/experiments/data_belay/accuracy.py#L99) scores the choice text after `Question: …\nAnswer:`. lm-eval's `mmlu` scores lettered choices.
- [`_piqa`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ba30b94916cc174ad0b2786651f94c8e88e88235/experiments/data_belay/accuracy.py#L90) uses lm-eval's `Question:/Answer:` prompt. The Eval Policy PIQA answer task (#10197) uses `Goal:/Solution:`, so Data Belay scores PIQA's answer BPB under one prompt and its accuracy under the other.

The verdict reads choice loss for MMLU-Pro and TruthfulQA only ([`CHOICE_TASKS`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ba30b94916cc174ad0b2786651f94c8e88e88235/experiments/data_belay/judge.py#L53)), with the Eval Policy answer tasks' prompts. The other seven tasks feed the README's accuracy check. `LevanterHarnessLM` runs a Levanter model with named axes. The grug `Transformer` that Data Belay trains is plain JAX, so it needs an adapter.

Done when:
- `data-belay score` writes choice loss and accuracy through `LevanterHarnessLM`, and `accuracy.py` has no scorer of its own.
- Data Belay scores PIQA under one prompt.
- On an existing run, MMLU-Pro's and TruthfulQA's choice loss match the current scorer's, or the README states the difference.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

The open [Data Belay PR #11019](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11019) owns the scorer, so this is follow-up work after that PR lands. Levanter's harness expects named tensors and packed attention masks, while the trained Grug `Transformer` uses plain JAX arrays and a different attention mask. The current score also depends on a seeded sample of at most 2,000 rows and byte-normalized accuracy; stock lm-eval task settings would change those measurements.

**Relevant code**
- [`accuracy.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ba30b94916cc174ad0b2786651f94c8e88e88235/experiments/data_belay/accuracy.py#L120) — current choice scoring and prompts.
- [`eval_harness.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/levanter/src/levanter/eval_harness.py#L220) — named model and packed requests.
- [`eval_policy_answer_bpb.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ba30b94916cc174ad0b2786651f94c8e88e88235/experiments/datasets/eval_policy_answer_bpb.py#L99) — PIQA prompt and sample policy.
- [`results.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ba30b94916cc174ad0b2786651f94c8e88e88235/experiments/data_belay/results.py#L44) — durable `TaskScore` format.
- [`judge.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ba30b94916cc174ad0b2786651f94c8e88e88235/experiments/data_belay/judge.py#L53) — verdict reads two choice metrics.

# Proposed Fix

## Design

After #11019 merges, add a thin Equinox adapter around the Grug checkpoint for `run_lm_eval_harness`. It should expose the named position, embedding, and vocabulary axes expected by Levanter, convert packed token and segment arrays to Grug's JAX inputs and attention mask, then return named activations and the language-model head. Keep checkpoint loading and score submission in Data Belay; use Levanter's harness for request packing and log-likelihoods.

Define lm-eval multiple-choice tasks for the existing nine datasets. Pin each dataset revision, split, and the current seed-0 sample of at most 2,000 rows. Use lm-eval's HellaSwag cleanup and MMLU letter choices; use Eval Policy's `Goal:/Solution:` prompt for PIQA. Keep MMLU-Pro and TruthfulQA (MC1) on their existing Eval Policy prompts and full answer-text choices, since their `choice_bits` feed the verdict. Extend Levanter's task configuration with dataset revision, document preprocessing, and a per-question metric hook: compute `−log2 softmax(ll)[gold]` from harness log-likelihoods and keep `acc_norm` normalized by UTF-8 bytes. This avoids a second model scorer while preserving the metrics' definitions.

Change `data-belay score` to load each finished run's final checkpoint, call the harness, and write the same `TaskScore` fields consumed by `report`; remove the scorer in `accuracy.py` and update the CLI target. Write the new scores under a versioned prefix, and require a complete, consistently scored control/treatment set before computing a verdict. Existing JSON must not silently mix with new scores.

## Validation

Test task prompts, gold labels, sample identities, and the choice metric on small fixed examples. On one H100, compare adapter log-likelihoods with the current scorer for a packed batch with multiple segments, then score an existing checkpoint through both paths. Compare MMLU-Pro and TruthfulQA `choice_bits`; if they differ, record the sizes and causes in the README, including any verdict change. Refresh the README's accuracy table if its checkpoints remain; otherwise label it as legacy and add a new table from consistently rescored arms. Run Data Belay and Levanter harness tests before a PR with `Fixes #11478`.

## Open question

Some stored scores may outlive their checkpoints. Should historical reports retain a clearly labeled legacy-score view for those runs, or require full rescoring before comparison? The proposed default is to require a complete new-version arm for any new verdict.

issues.title: [data_belay] Score choice loss and accuracy with LevanterHarnessLM

issues.author: ravwojdyla-agent
issues.body:
Data Belay (#11019) judges a candidate's harm against dilution references: four Datakit sources whose text no eval measures (ClimbLab Japanese, and FinePDFs Chinese, Thai and Arabic), trained at the candidate's share. They measure what giving up that share of the base mix costs on its own. On main's model, giving up 20% costs each eval group 1.3% to 3.6%. References exist only at 20% ([`DILUTION_REFERENCES`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/9be1e608da27271e669dce3e9e9557189e29f237/experiments/data_belay/results.py#L29)). `report` refuses a candidate at any other share unless `--against` is given, and prints the `prepare-datakit` commands that build the references at that share. Users should be able to choose the share, so the set of shares with references has to grow as shares get used.

A share costs 12 reference runs per rung (4 references × 3 seeds), where a candidate costs 3. Each reference also needs its own cache at the share, because `prepare-datakit` sizes a cache for one share and names its runs by it. The references belong to one model and base mix, like the controls, and need retraining when either changes.

Done when:
- One command prepares, trains and scores the four references at a given share and rung.
- `check --share` accepts shares from a fixed grid, for example 5, 10, 20, 35 and 50%, so that references get reused. For a share without references, it says how many reference runs the share needs.
- References at a rung are trained when the first candidate at that share reaches the rung, so d1024 references are trained only for shares that get there.
- `report` judges a candidate at any share in the grid that has references.

Not tested: whether the dilution cost interpolates between shares. If it does, references at a few shares could cover the shares between them.
