issues.author: hammer
issues.body:
Other groups cannot check or reuse Marin's eval results. Each eval run writes a `record.json` ([`records.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/e9ae26899c90512195e68f0edec808bb42b88bf3/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/records.py#L1-L13)) to `gs://marin-eval-metadata/evals` or a CoreWeave bucket. EvalDash, Marin's eval dashboard, reads these records behind Marina sign-in.

Published results go out as markdown tables in Hugging Face model cards (`marin-community/marin-8b-base`, `marin-8b-instruct`, `marin-32b-base`) or as issue comments and gists. For example, the eval-policy results for `open-athena/Marin-Snowball-67B-A2B-v0.1` ("Snowball v0.1") are in #10283. None of these four repos has eval results in a machine-readable form. To compare a Marin model with another model on the same benchmark, a reader copies numbers by hand. The copied numbers do not carry the prompt format, sampling settings or harness version behind them.

The [EvalEval Coalition](https://evalevalai.com) maintains [Every Eval Ever](https://github.com/evaleval/every_eval_ever) (EEE), an MIT-licensed JSON schema for eval results. An EEE record holds:

- the source and the evaluator's relationship to the model developer (`source_metadata`)
- each score with its metric definition and generation settings (`evaluation_results`)
- an optional per-sample JSONL file

Records go into the public [`evaleval/EEE_datastore`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/evaleval/EEE_datastore) dataset. EvalEval's [Evaluation Cards](https://evalcards.evalevalai.com) read that datastore and plot each model's scores next to other models' scores on the same benchmark. [Hugging Face Community Evals](https://huggingface.co/blog/eee-community-evals) shows scores on model cards through `.eval_results/*.yaml` files that link back to the EEE record; for now it covers MMLU-Pro, GPQA, HLE and GSM8K. EEE ships converters for lm-evaluation-harness, Inspect and HELM logs, and a `validate` command.

Swiss AI used this setup for [Apertus 1.5](https://evalevalai.com/infrastructure/2026/10/15/apertus-open-reproducible-evals/). It published 48 benchmarks for the 8B model and 47 for the 70B model as EEE records, produced with its public lm-evaluation-harness fork, and they appear on Evaluation Cards.

Marin's eval policy (#10197) defines the benchmarks, harness settings and commits behind Marin's public eval results, and ships as dated releases. Its records already hold most of what EEE asks for:

- the model revision
- generation settings (`ModelGenerationConfig`) and serving settings (`ServingParams`)
- the git SHA and eval runtime
- per-task metrics

Two problems remain besides the format.

- Published scores do not show their sampling settings. Snowball v0.1 was [evaluated at T=1.0 / top_p=1.0 by mistake](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10283#issuecomment-6659903935): its `generation_config.json` set no sampling defaults, and the pinned Evalchemy dropped `temperature`. The baselines ran at their own shipped defaults. The original results in #10283 did not state any of these settings, and all 26 benchmarks had to be re-run. A published record that carries the generation settings next to each score lets anyone see such a mismatch.
- Records name the user who submitted the launch, but not the evaluating organization or its relationship to the model developer. Marin evaluates other developers' models as baselines, so readers need to tell Marin's own results apart from third-party results.

Done when:

- An exporter converts a Marin `record.json`, and its per-sample outputs where they exist, into EEE aggregate and sample files. It covers Evalchemy, Harbor and legacy lm-evaluation-harness runs, and the output passes EEE's `validate`.
- Exported records state the effective sampling settings (temperature, top_p, max tokens, chat template arguments). They also name the evaluating organization and its relationship to the model developer.
- The next eval-policy release publishes EEE records for every Marin model and baseline in the release. They go to `evaleval/EEE_datastore`, or to a public Hugging Face dataset linked from the release.
- The four model repos above carry `.eval_results/*.yaml` entries for the benchmarks Community Evals supports, each linking to its EEE record.
- The eval policy document states that policy results are published in EEE format.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

`record.json` carries task metrics, model configuration, evaluator pin, and result paths, but the [record writer](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/runner.py#L142) does not capture the effective sampling settings. [Evalchemy clamps the output-token budget at execution](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evalchemy/client.py#L107), and model/server defaults can supply temperature and top-p, so a later export cannot safely reconstruct them from launch configuration. Existing [lm-eval sample sources](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/lm_eval_samples.py#L316) and [Harbor samples](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/runner.py#L193) are stored in finestore, but EEE requires separate aggregate JSON and optional sample JSONL with matching IDs and paths. No overlapping open PR appeared in searches for `11489`, `Every Eval Ever`, or `evaleval`.

**Relevant code**
- [`records.py#L90`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/records.py#L90) — normalized generation overrides.
- [`records.py#L267`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/records.py#L267) — durable run record.
- [`client.py#L107`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evalchemy/client.py#L107) — effective Evalchemy command.
- [`harbor/runner.py#L193`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/runner.py#L193) — agentic sample archive.

# Proposed Fix

1. Resolve and capture typed effective settings from Evalchemy and Harbor requests plus checkpoint and serving defaults: temperature, top-p, max tokens, chat-template arguments, and the source of each value. Add evaluating organization and its first- or third-party relationship to the model developer. Historical values stay unknown unless preserved request logs or artifacts prove them.
2. Export selected successful runs from `record.json` and finestore into EEE aggregate JSON and sample JSONL. Map each task/metric to a benchmark and metric definition; preserve model revision, evaluator commit, source run ID, and sample identity. Reuse [EEE's lm-eval converter](https://github.com/evaleval/every_eval_ever#-eval-converters) where it retains those fields; add a Harbor adapter for trial rewards and agentic traces. Reject missing required settings and unmapped metrics explicitly.
3. Test representative Evalchemy, legacy lm-eval, and Harbor records against [EEE validation](https://github.com/evaleval/every_eval_ever#-data-validation), including aggregate/sample links and row counts. Freeze the next [eval-policy](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10197) release's selected run IDs and hashes; recover settings from durable evidence or rerun unverifiable cells, then publish the validated records to EEE's datastore or a linked public dataset. Stream only selected artifacts.
4. Generate Community Evals `.eval_results/*.yaml` from the published records for the three `marin-community` model repos and `open-athena/Marin-Snowball-67B-A2B-v0.1`, using only supported benchmarks, and update the policy text with the EEE publication rule and record links.

Release owners need to choose the public dataset destination and confirm the exact release cells, corrected scores, and model-repo revisions before publication. This spans record capture, three exporter paths, release selection, external dataset publication, and four model repos, so it needs staged changes rather than one small PR.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
## TL;DR

On the same data (Experiment 2's 216 pinned SFT chat caches, 234,383,016,035 real tokens after 262,144-token left-slicing), Levanter's sequential packer produces 1,035,158 sequences at 13.6267% padding with the 64-segment cap. A bounded-window first-fit lookahead packer removes 42% of that padding (970,215 sequences, 7.8451% at window 64) with local reordering and a few CPU-seconds of packing cost. What remains is set by the segment cap, not document order: raising the cap is a separate lever (cap 128 + lookahead → 2.45% chat padding, cap 256 → 1.33%, uncapped → 0.98%). Recommendation: adopt the lookahead packer as an opt-in option (PR #11379), decide the segment cap separately in Experiment 3, keep replay leaves streamed.

## Description

Experiment 2 SFT packs whole conversations into 262,144-token sequences on 216 chat leaves (`pack=True` → at most 64 segments per sequence); 1,711 pretraining-replay leaves run as a continuous stream (no packing, documents cross sequence boundaries with EOS). Conversations are never split, so each sequence pads the tail it cannot fill. The question: how much of that padding is recoverable by a better packer on the same data, at what cost?

Method: per-document token lengths were re-extracted offsets-only from the pinned caches (every cache verified against the Experiment 2 census receipts: rows, tokens, per-cache length-vector SHA-256; totals 21,245,136 traces / 234,420,759,584 tokens). Packing strategies were simulated offline on CPU; no model, no training run, no source data change. Pretraining-replay leaf caches were extracted the same way from the pinned spec (388 leaves, 35,255,949 documents, 38,826,415,376 tokens).

Run-wide composition context for interpreting the totals:

- 128-sequence prefix estimates from the native loader: 22 replay / 106 chat; 30,847,679 real tokens of 33,554,432 positions (8.07% padding overall; chat 9.74%; replay 0%).
- Expected composition (weights × component stats), phase 0: replay 20.47% of positions, 22.33% of real tokens, 29.92% of loss-bearing tokens; chat assistant tokens are 67.34% of chat real tokens. Phase 1 (from step 8000): replay 20.37% / 22.22% / 29.79%.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Measure, per packing strategy, the pad fraction overall and per source, packed sequences (equivalently optimizer updates at batch 8), segments per sequence, reorder distance against the source order, packing compute/memory cost, and determinism/resumability; and quantify how much padding the 64-segment cap versus document order causes.

## Status

Complete. Strategies measured at capacity 262,144, cap 64, packing within each child cache, `slice_strategy="left"` for over-long documents. Real tokens are identical in every row; positions and padding vary.

| Packer | Packed sequences | Positions | Pad fraction | Relative change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| sequential (Levanter's current, baseline) | 1,035,158 | 271,360,458,752 | 13.6267% | — |
| lookahead w=8 | 979,589 | 256,793,378,816 | 8.7270% | −39.4% |
| lookahead w=64 | 970,215 | 254,336,040,960 | 7.8451% | −42.4% |
| lookahead w=256 | 968,405 | 253,861,560,320 | 7.6729% | −43.7% |
| lookahead w=1024 | 967,574 | 253,643,718,656 | 7.5936% | −44.3% |
| window FFD w=64 | 1,063,698 | 278,842,048,512 | 15.9442% | worse |
| window FFD w=1024 | 999,300 | 261,960,499,200 | 10.5273% | worse |
| window BFD w=1024 | 999,291 | 261,958,139,904 | 10.5265% | worse |
| global best-fit-decreasing | 989,596 | 259,416,653,824 | 9.6500% | worse |
| lower bound (cap 64) | 961,454 | 252,039,397,376 | 7.0006% | floor |

Segment-cap binding (definition: a 64-document pack that still had room for the next document): 143,933 of 1,035,158 packs (13.904%); 46 of 184 SFT components bind, led by math_v2/low, instruction_following_chat_v2, identity-data, ultrachat (≥99.4%). With the cap, 99.9% of the lower-bound padding comes from the 39 cap-bound sources; per-source group split: cap-bound sources 45.75% → 45.72% padding (unchanged by any packer), non-cap-bound sources 8.29% → 1.06%.

Reorder distance (share of documents moved / mean displacement in positions): lookahead w=8: 14.5% / 0.31 (max 29); w=64: 35.2% / 1.55 (max 63); w=1024: 53.1% / 12.37; global BFD: full re-sort. Because cross-document attention is blocked, reordering changes sequence/batch composition, not per-document computation; source composition per sequence is invariant and per-batch composition is unchanged in distribution; under fixed per-sequence mixture weights, per-source real-token shares shift at most +0.37 pp.

Packer cost (single CPU core, all 21.2M documents): sequential 1.5 s; lookahead w=8/64/256/1024 = 7.0/10.5/22.2/70.1 s; window FFD/BFD 42–54 s; global BFD 50 s. Memory O(n) (two int64 arrays; ≤58 MB on the largest cache). All strategies are deterministic and rebuild identically from the cache after a restart.

Segment-cap axis (chat pad fraction, sequential → lookahead w=64): cap 64: 13.6267% → 7.8451%; cap 128: 8.9632% → 2.4478%; cap 256: 7.9986% → 1.3325%; cap 512: 7.8221% → 1.1293%; uncapped: 7.6911% → 0.9787%. Cost of a larger cap: no training-path array is shaped by `max_segments` (segment ids and FA4/CuTe bounds are per-token `[B, S]` int32/bool; short-conv kernels likewise), so raising it costs zero training memory; only eval per-segment metrics allocate a `(max_Segments, Pos)` mask. Chat fully streamed (documents crossing sequences) would be 894,348 sequences / 0.0116% padding — the absolute floor, at the cost of cross-conversation attention.

Replay leaves: streamed continuously in the consumed configuration, 148,311 sequences, 0.1348% padding (2,699 documents exceed 262,144 and are split, not truncated). Packing replay with the chat packer would instead produce 579,303 sequences at 76.21% padding. Combined consumed-configuration view: chat sequential + replay stream = 310,239,297,536 positions at 11.9359% padding; chat lookahead w=64 + replay stream = 293,214,879,744 positions at 6.8228% padding.

Validation: the offline simulation matches Levanter's reference `pack_documents` exactly on 200 randomized inputs × 3 segment caps, and the PR's lookahead implementation produces exactly the same packs as the simulation on five real caches (largest 3.6M documents, plus segment-cap-bound and small caches).

## Links

* Full report: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/benfeuer/sft-new-mix-candidate/packing-ablation/REPORT.md` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/benfeuer/sft-new-mix-candidate/packing-ablation/REPORT.md))
* Result JSONs (per-strategy/per-cache/per-source, cap sweep, cap binding, replay side): same prefix ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/benfeuer/sft-new-mix-candidate/packing-ablation/))
* Opt-in packer implementation: PR #11379
* Experiment 2 census inputs: `artifacts/experiment2/population-262k-final/truncation-census.json` (216 chat caches) and the pinned spec's `pretrain/*` replay components

## Decision Log

* 2026-11-13: measured; baseline reproduces the Experiment 2 population census exactly (1,035,158 sequences, 13.6267%). Windowed decreasing and global BFD rejected (worse than lookahead under the segment cap). Lookahead packer implemented as opt-in; Experiment 2 keeps its current packer.
* 2026-11-13: replay leaves confirmed continuous-stream in the consumed config; `pack: 262144` literals in the pinned component JSONs are historical and unconsumed.

## Conclusion

Packing efficiency on this corpus is bounded first by the 64-segment cap and second by document order. A bounded-window lookahead removes 39–42% of chat padding at trivial cost with local reordering, and reaches within 0.85 pp of the cap-64 floor. The remaining ~7% padding under the current cap requires raising the segment cap (a data/training decision, zero training-memory cost) rather than a different packer. Replay stays streamed.

issues.author: rdolmedo
issues.body:
🤖 Pre-registered prediction of Snowball's TB2.1 (Terminal-Bench 2.1, 89 tasks) loss and pass@1 after 10.51B SFT tokens, from Snowflake. Recorded before any Snowball TB2.1 number was looked at.

**SFT.** Snowflake d512 / d768 / d1024 were SFT'd as in #10753 (Snowball's SFT recipe, LR checked per model with the same rule), at Snowball's TB SFT budgets of 0.3 / 0.71 / 1.7 / 4.0 / 10.5B tokens (15 cells). The exceptions are the context, 16 × 131K tokens per step instead of 64 × 32K (the same 2.1M tokens per step), and d768's LR, which the check moved from 1e-3 to 1.5e-3. A follow-up comment will give more details on the SFT data: tasks generated by DeepSeek, trajectories generated by Nemotron Super.

## Loss

TB2.1 test loss = bits per byte on Nemotron Super trajectories for the TB2.1 tasks (266 documents). Laws from the #10753 pre-registration, fitted on the 15 Snowflake cells with summed pre-training compute and the floor E free in [0, 0.99 × min L] (every fit puts E at 0), least squares on log L.

| Law | Role | **TB2.1 loss at 10.51B** |
|---|---|---|
| **Baseline** (3 rungs at the target budget) | **headline: simplest, held on SWE** | **0.2197** |
| **L1** | second: the SWE headline law | **0.2222** |
| L4 | reference | 0.2252 |
| L6 | reference | 0.2276 |

Baseline law: L(C) = 0.3621 · (C / 1.212e21)^−0.1017, with C = summed pre-training FLOPs (Snowball: 1.650e23).

## pass@1

Abilities θ come from a joint 1PL (Rasch) fit on TB2.1 plus 65 TB-Lite tasks, 5 attempts per task. θ is regressed on TB2.1 loss L by weighted least squares (weights 1/SE²), and

TB2.1 pass@1(L) = (1/89) Σ_i sigmoid(θ(L) − b_i), with b_i the fitted difficulties of the 89 TB2.1 tasks.

- **Link: Snowball 7% (headline):** θ = 11.78 − 52.85 · L. Fitted on Snowball's step-18000 checkpoint (7% of training) after 1B and 3B SFT tokens (pass@1 1.6% and 5.2%).
- **Link: Snowflake d1024 + Qwen 4B (second):** θ = 6.69 − 31.33 · L. Fitted on d1024 after 1.7B / 4.0B / 10.5B SFT tokens (0.0% / 0.4% / 0.7%) and Qwen3.5-4B after 4B SFT tokens (22.5%).

| Loss prediction | TB2.1 loss | **Link: Snowball 7%** | Link: Snowflake d1024 + Qwen 4B |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Baseline (headline)** | 0.2197 | **23.1%** [12.6, 38.9] | **20.0%** [14.9, 26.3] |

Brackets: 95% task-bootstrap intervals (TB2.1 and TB-Lite tasks resampled, Rasch fit and link refit per draw). They cover the link only, not the loss prediction.

![TB2.1 pre-registration](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/rdolmedo/0c14b1140a88c50c12700a6dd45920cc/raw/tb_prereg_figure.png)

comments.body:
🤖 **SFT-only prediction, 2026-11-13**, recorded before any 10.5B result was looked at. We have a synthetic data generation pipeline (tasks generated by DeepSeek, trajectories by Nemotron Super), and we would like to know whether performance increases predictably as we synthesize and train on more data. So we also predict Snowball's 10.5B point from its own SFT checkpoints at 0.3 / 0.71 / 1.7 / 4.0B tokens, with no Snowflake input:

- **Ability:** θ = 4.89 − 20.67 · L, fitted on the checkpoints' TB2.1-only abilities (difficulties b_i as in the amendment); pass@1 = (1/89) Σ_i sigmoid(θ − b_i).

| SFT tokens | TB2.1 loss | TB2.1 pass@1 |
|---|---|---|
| **10.5B (predicted)** | **0.2064** | **26.0%** [19.5, 32.9] |

Brackets: 95% bootstrap over TB2.1 tasks, ability step only.

![SFT-only prediction](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/rdolmedo/0c14b1140a88c50c12700a6dd45920cc/raw/tb_sft_only.png)

comments.author: rdolmedo
comments.body:
🤖 **Result.** Snowball after 10.51B SFT tokens: TB2.1 test loss **0.2058**, TB2.1 pass@1 **27.0%** (120/445 attempts, 5 per task).

The amended headline predicted 28.9%, **1.9 pp** above the result. That closeness is misleading: both halves of the prediction missed by a lot, in opposite directions, and the errors cancelled.

- **Loss:** the baseline law predicted 0.2197, **+6.8%** above the measured 0.2058. The other laws were further off: L1 +8.0%, L4 +9.4%, L6 +10.6%.
- **Links, evaluated at the measured loss (0.2058):**

| Link | pass@1 at the measured loss | Error |
|---|---|---|
| Snowball 7% (headline) | 38.2% | **+11.2 pp** |
| Snowflake d1024 + Qwen 4B (second) | 23.6% | **−3.4 pp** |

![TB2.1 pre-registration (amended) and result](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/rdolmedo/0c14b1140a88c50c12700a6dd45920cc/raw/tb_prereg_figure_amended_result.png)

comments.author: rdolmedo
comments.body:
**What could we have done differently?**

**Loss.** This is not a problem with the law: the ~136× extrapolation past d1024 is simply large. The registered law's ±1 SE at Snowball is ±6.9% (3 points, 1 df), and the measured loss falls inside it. One additional point, say ~20× from Snowball, should probably already give the correction we need. I tried several other laws (the registered L1–L6, a free floor, other compute axes) and none convinced me more than the standard one. The solution is just to extrapolate less.

**Link.** Two SFT budgets were too few, and the fitted link happened to be very optimistic. With one more SFT budget (step-18000 at 6B SFT tokens), the link no longer overshoots: at the measured loss it gives 25.1% (measured 27.0%), against 38.9% with two budgets. This requires having checkpoints of Snowball (step-18000 is still ~16× less compute than Snowball). Using Qwen 4B as the anchor instead (link 2) only needs the Snowflake models, but comes out a bit short: 23.4% at the measured loss. (These post-hoc links are fit on the TB2.1 eval's own attempts only; the amended links also pooled tbmix's attempts on its 35 TB2.1 tasks.)

![TB2.1 post-hoc](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/rdolmedo/0c14b1140a88c50c12700a6dd45920cc/raw/tb_posthoc_prediction_tb21eval.png)

comments.author: rdolmedo
comments.body:
🤖 **SFT-only prediction: result.** It worked quite well, but it was only a ~3× extrapolation (4.0B → 10.5B SFT tokens).

| | Predicted | Measured |
|---|---|---|
| TB2.1 loss | 0.2064 | 0.2058 (+0.3%) |
| TB2.1 pass@1 | 26.8% | 27.0% (−0.2 pp) |

The posted pass@1 (26.0%) had a bug: the ability fit pooled tbmix's attempts on 35 TB2.1 tasks instead of using the TB2.1 eval only, as intended. With the pre-registered methodology implemented correctly, the prediction is 26.8%.

![SFT-only result](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/rdolmedo/0c14b1140a88c50c12700a6dd45920cc/raw/tb_sft_only_result.png)

comments.author: rdolmedo
comments.body:
**How much will more SFT data help?** We generate the SFT data synthetically, so we could scale it up arbitrarily. Fitting all five SFT budgets (0.3–10.5B tokens) and extrapolating to 100B: TB2.1 loss 0.185 (0.206 at 10.5B) and pass@1 ~33% (32.6% ± 2.7 pp on the 89 TB2.1 tasks, 27.0% at 10.5B). That is, ~10× more SFT data buys ~6 pp; the scaling is disappointingly slow (and slower still if the loss has a floor, which these five points cannot rule out).

![TB2.1 SFT scaling to 100B](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/rdolmedo/0c14b1140a88c50c12700a6dd45920cc/raw/tb_sft_5pt_100b.png)

comments.author: rdolmedo
comments.body:
Overall takeaway: the approach used for SWE-bench continues to work for tbench. However, tbench gives little signal at the snowflake scales, and we had to use the 7% Snowball intermediate checkpoint.

To set expectations, >100x extrapolations may carry a substantial amount of error, and require external models (e.g., Qwen 3.5 4B) as anchors. Nonetheless, ~20x extrapolations seem to be feasible. Meaning, for example, to extrapolate from Snowball to Mochi.

Next step: predict Snowball's post-SFT performance on an open reproduction of the AAI index.

comments.author: rdolmedo
comments.body:
🤖 **The same fit against B200-hours.** Synthesizing the data (tasks from DeepSeek, trajectories from Nemotron Super; 2 traces per task, 2 epochs) costs ~27 B200-h per 1B SFT tokens at the latest pipeline's steady-state rates, and training Snowball adds ~15 (measured on these runs), so training is ~36% of the total. Spending 10k B200-h on synthesis (367B SFT tokens) predicts **36.0% ± 3.7** TB2.1 pass@1; spending 10k on synthesis and training together (236B SFT tokens) predicts **34.9% ± 3.3**. The band includes the uncertainty of both the loss law and the link.

issues.body:
## TL;DR

The Atlas curriculum audit reproduced all counts across 4,206,876 tasks and found that the original distance cutoffs reject almost every capability placement. The experiment retains nearest-node placement and exports five selectable similarity levels. The chosen default assigns all tasks; stricter levels expose the existing scores without new embeddings or rankings. These are approximate labels, and better task descriptions and embeddings remain follow-up work.

A task's subject score is its cosine similarity to the nearest broad subject anchor. Its capability score is the best similarity to a specific operation within that chosen subject. Groups are navigation nodes between subjects and capabilities. The five display levels filter these two stored scores.

## Description

[#10157](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10157), merged October 15, 2026, introduced maximum cosine distances of 0.45 for subject membership and 0.25 for capability placement. Those correspond to minimum similarities of 0.55 and 0.75. In the current 310-source population, only 23,956 tasks have a capability placement, 2,744,320 have only a subject, and 1,438,600 fall outside the subject cutoff. Every one of the 45 domains has more than 96% subject-only placement among its subject members.

The full scan exactly reconciled every source denominator, outcome, and curriculum-node count. Capability scores are generally higher than membership scores: the median paired difference is positive in every domain. Domain capability medians range from 0.612 to 0.669, well below the 0.75 gate. For Earth sciences, membership median is 0.586; capability p05/median/p95 is 0.559/0.622/0.688. Only 10 of 7,088 Earth members pass the original capability gate.

The adopted taxonomy projects exactly to all 45 subjects (domains), 406 groups, and 1,999 capabilities. Earth's single immediate child is an authored wrapper above seven subgroups and 37 capabilities. No taxonomy nodes were truncated. Earth has 182 sampled subject-only tasks. Among 5,841 source/domain combinations with subject-only tasks, 3,456 lack a stored example, covering 117,321 instances; population counts are complete.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Retain approximate nearest subject and capability labels for every task, and let readers choose how strictly to filter the stored similarities. Precomputed counts and scored examples should make confidence changes entirely client-side. The level names describe display filters, not calibrated probabilities of correctness.

| Display level | Subject minimum similarity | Capability minimum similarity | Tasks with both | Fraction of all tasks |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| All (nearest), default | 0.30 | 0.30 | 4,206,876 | 100.000% |
| Broad | 0.55 | 0.60 | 2,416,638 | 57.445% |
| Moderate | 0.55 | 0.65 | 1,262,536 | 30.011% |
| Strict | 0.55 | 0.70 | 311,593 | 7.407% |
| Original (#10157) | 0.55 | 0.75 | 23,956 | 0.569% |

These fractions are measured counterfactuals from the complete stored-score population. The minimum observed primary subject and capability similarities are 0.347478 and 0.359608, so the default's maximum distances of 0.70/0.70 place the complete current population. Its unassigned fraction is zero. The 1,438,600 previously outside the subject gate also receive approximate labels. At each stricter level they remain Unplaced; tasks that pass only the subject gate become Other/unlisted (subject only).

## Status

The score scan and taxonomy/sample checks are complete. The nearest-placement export has completed with 4,206,876 assigned tasks and zero unassigned tasks. All five confidence count vectors and the combined scored example export are complete. The union contains 74,582 tasks in 88,278,132 Parquet bytes. Every nonempty curriculum node at every level has at least min(10, population) sampled examples. All/train/eval vectors exactly match an independent aggregation. The original artifacts are preserved. Producer commit [2f8025cae8](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/2f8025cae8034d87ea80f74c11b3fbbfab20da05) passed lint/type checks, advisory review, and 72 producer/projection/catalog tests before landing. The implementation adds cumulative per-source/node count vectors and samples each curriculum node independently at every level before combining the samples. Sample rows retain the original membership and capability similarities. No task vectors or rankings are recomputed.

The main quality limitation is the representation: direct-text mode embeds up to 8 KiB of public prompts and public answer/tool requirements against operation-focused capability anchors. Inspected mismatches include unrelated few-shot/history text routed to Earth and factual recall mapped to an analytical operation. The audit has not isolated how much each representation choice contributes. Exploratory examples include an Earth-season question nearest to geologic chronology at 0.595 and a winter-solstice question nearest to tidal prediction at 0.642. Lowering a cutoff increases coverage without establishing semantic correctness. Improving embeddings and operation-centered task descriptions is explicit follow-up work.

The four successful regional CPU jobs used 46.892 requested CPU-hours (CPU request × task runtime, excluding queue time) and 1.591 measured producer-process CPU-hours. No GPUs, new embeddings, or ranking computations were used. The five-level sample Parquet is 88.28 MB; its pre-aggregated confidence sidecar is 13.52 MB. Old artifacts remain unchanged; the final metadata seal records the export version and canonical level identity over the same verified numeric outputs.

## Links

- Alignment release: `s3://marin-rno2a/marin/rl-data/atlas-curriculum-audit/2026.11.14.4/confidence-five-sealed-v1/release.json` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-rno2a%2Fmarin%2Frl-data%2Fatlas-curriculum-audit%2F2026.11.14.4%2Fconfidence-five-sealed-v1%2Frelease.json)); SHA-256 `a67d5670875ddc21d425aacab31a687f3a1ea26484907e64c30330b221fdb8e4`.
- Five-level coverage: `s3://marin-rno2a/marin/rl-data/atlas-curriculum-audit/2026.11.14.4/confidence-five-sealed-v1/coverage.json` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-rno2a%2Fmarin%2Frl-data%2Fatlas-curriculum-audit%2F2026.11.14.4%2Fconfidence-five-sealed-v1%2Fcoverage.json)); SHA-256 `e3d63798d5c0b6b1f30cfe5b2e4caf2cb35e34e0413f51c6a2f7d701e6b40757`.
- Confidence sidecar: `s3://marin-rno2a/marin/rl-data/atlas-curriculum-audit/2026.11.14.4/confidence-five-sealed-v1/confidence.json` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-rno2a%2Fmarin%2Frl-data%2Fatlas-curriculum-audit%2F2026.11.14.4%2Fconfidence-five-sealed-v1%2Fconfidence.json)); SHA-256 `d40c4ecdb2eb502bd5cf5f49f35bb1700f42ecd71ffd7f544f90b802d07a2cb4`.
- Verified experiment receipt: `s3://marin-rno2a/marin/rl-data/atlas-curriculum-audit/2026.11.14.4/confidence-five-sealed-v1/experiment-receipt.json` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-rno2a%2Fmarin%2Frl-data%2Fatlas-curriculum-audit%2F2026.11.14.4%2Fconfidence-five-sealed-v1%2Fexperiment-receipt.json)); SHA-256 `6efa4fb31fca8e9ab4f4f3523612e35f93697302eb76e0707a3b1a8f89f31acf`.
- Structured handoff and field shape: `s3://marin-rno2a/marin/rl-data/atlas-curriculum-audit/2026.11.14.4/confidence-five-sealed-v1/handoff-v1.json` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-rno2a%2Fmarin%2Frl-data%2Fatlas-curriculum-audit%2F2026.11.14.4%2Fconfidence-five-sealed-v1%2Fhandoff-v1.json)).
- Compute details: `s3://marin-rno2a/marin/rl-data/atlas-curriculum-audit/2026.11.14.4/confidence-five-sealed-v1/compute-final-v1.json` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-rno2a%2Fmarin%2Frl-data%2Fatlas-curriculum-audit%2F2026.11.14.4%2Fconfidence-five-sealed-v1%2Fcompute-final-v1.json)).
- Remote readback and identity verification: `s3://marin-rno2a/marin/rl-data/atlas-curriculum-audit/2026.11.14.4/confidence-five-sealed-v1/final-readback-verification-v1.json` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-rno2a%2Fmarin%2Frl-data%2Fatlas-curriculum-audit%2F2026.11.14.4%2Fconfidence-five-sealed-v1%2Ffinal-readback-verification-v1.json)).
- Reference documentation: [Curriculum coverage](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/2f8025cae8034d87ea80f74c11b3fbbfab20da05/docs/references/rl-data-atlas.md#curriculum-coverage).
- Integration: [#11277](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11277).
- Original implementation: [#10157](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10157).
- Full distributions, coverage curve, reconciliation and compute: `s3://marin-rno2a/marin/rl-data/atlas-curriculum-audit/2026.11.14.1/score-audit-v1.json` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-rno2a%2Fmarin%2Frl-data%2Fatlas-curriculum-audit%2F2026.11.14.1%2Fscore-audit-v1.json)); SHA-256 `8ea56f118533d2972b15020fea38b5ed67dc07e86f2be8e0b3ba44704f79a415`.
- Sample audit and exploratory examples: `s3://marin-rno2a/marin/rl-data/atlas-curriculum-audit/2026.11.14.1/sample-audit-v1.json` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-rno2a%2Fmarin%2Frl-data%2Fatlas-curriculum-audit%2F2026.11.14.1%2Fsample-audit-v1.json)); SHA-256 `c8dcce4fb4391ba99786c5c94b07ded2ec8a1ca0e10dad275d6f53a23a0343f7`.
- Runnable scan scripts and source hashes: the same artifact prefix contains `measure_scores.py`, `measure_samples.py`, `taxonomy-verification.json`, and `audit-provenance.json`.

## Decision Log

- 2026-11-14: preserve the 0.45/0.25 distance baseline; use 0.70/0.70 distances for complete current-population placement.
- 2026-11-14: export five display levels and their counts so changing confidence requires no model inference or server-side scoring.
- 2026-11-14: seal and remotely verify the final manifests, preserve all original data, and deliver the scored sample union to the preview integration lane.

## Conclusion

The original capability gate explains the sparse placement counts; neither missing taxonomy nodes nor uniformly lower capability cosines explains them. The measured display levels span 100% to 0.569% capability placement. The export and sample-union checks are complete, and the producer commit and pinned manifests have been handed to the preview integration lane in #11277. The 0.70/0.70 distance default places the complete audited population while preserving the original scores and all historical artifacts. Improving task descriptions and embeddings remains follow-up work.

issues.body:
## TL;DR

Hero (Mochi, 535B-A23B MoE) BF16 vLLM decode on GB200 is step-latency bound. Per-step time stays at 56–78 ms from 1 to 128 sequences per DP engine, so output throughput rises almost linearly with batch size until `max_num_seqs` caps it. Raising `max_num_seqs` from 32 to 64 doubles throughput at 1,024 concurrent requests (+95% to +99% in three same-node pairs, about 500 → 1,000 output tokens/s/GPU). Correctness gates pass, and latency at lower concurrency is unchanged. `max_num_seqs` 128 reached 3.6–3.8× the baseline cap at 2,048 concurrent requests (1,839 output tokens/s/GPU on a fast node set). `max_num_seqs` 256 gains nothing more, because the KV cache fills at about 250 sequences of 1K tokens per engine. With 4K outputs the KV cache fills at about 100–128 sequences per engine: 96 per engine (1,536 in flight) gives about 1,540 output tokens/s/GPU without waiting, and 128 gives 1,785–1,850 while KV-bound (R11). The `0ac9dcb` wheel from #11241 is throughput-neutral against `3004cd8` and is the current baseline. TP2 from vllm#119, a 2,048 → 8,192 prefill budget, and the one-sided NVLink all-to-all did not improve this workload. Most of the decode step is host overhead from the eager ShortConv op between piecewise graphs; letting decode replay full CUDA graphs (a two-line fork guard relaxation, R12) cuts the step 2.0–3.8× and raises throughput 43% at 1,024 in flight, with all gates passing (an apparent long-prompt slowdown did not reproduce). On top of that, a tuned GB200 fused-MoE config (+7%, R14) and NCCL symmetric memory for the MoE collectives (+6%, R15) each add throughput at 1,024 in flight, and four API servers lift 2,048 in flight by 13% (R13), where one API server had become the limit. Stacked in an A/B/A run on a fast node set (R16), the full set reaches about 1,430 output tokens/s/GPU at 1,024 in flight and 2,390 at 2,048, against about 1,050 and 1,840 for the best PIECEWISE configuration (cross-run), at 18.6 ms/token for a single request.

## Description

The objective is output tokens/s per GPU under RL-rollout-like load, with time to first token (TTFT) and inter-token latency (ITL) as guardrails. Precision stays BF16; FP8 is out of scope for now.

Setup for every measurement below:

- Weights: the SFT checkpoint `step-400407` exported as BF16 safetensors (export schema 3), `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/exports/mochi-sft/hero-sft-fullab-step393k-v2/step-400407/2af3f828aa-cpu-a1` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Fmarin%2Fexports%2Fmochi-sft%2Fhero-sft-fullab-step393k-v2%2Fstep-400407%2F2af3f828aa-cpu-a1)). Router and experts are stored in placed order `1e80fa529585`.
- Serving: Marin vLLM fork release `marin-vllm-gpu-20261113-0ac9dcb157ee`, the #11241 pin (`3004cd8f1632` before it was accepted).
- Topology: one 4-node GB200 gang (16 GPUs) in one NVLink domain on cw-us-east-08a, TP1 / DP16 / EP16, all-to-all `allgather_reducescatter`, Triton MoE, FlashInfer attention.
- Batching and context: `max_num_seqs` 32, `max_num_batched_tokens` 2,048, prefix caching off, `max_model_len` 262,144, one API server.
- Compilation: PIECEWISE CUDA graphs with `splitting_ops` = `unified_attention_with_output`, `unified_kv_cache_update`, `grug_moe_short_conv`.

This is the same configuration as the team's BF16 serving endpoint for the checkpoint (`hero-sft-step400407-bf16`). Its batch-1 decode reproduces that endpoint's logged ITL: 56 ms here against 58 ms.

Load: 1,024 GSM8K test questions with the Marin chat template (mean prompt 70 tokens), temperature 1.0, a fixed seed per request, `ignore_eos`, 1,024 output tokens per request. The loop is closed: the generator keeps a fixed number of requests in flight, three waves per point. Throughput is the output-token rate from when all in-flight requests have produced their first token until the last submission, divided by 16 GPUs. A batch-1 point (8 × 256 tokens) gives single-request latency.

Each candidate runs on the same 4 nodes as its control, back to back in one job. GB200 node sets on the cluster differ by about 20% in throughput for identical software, so unpaired comparisons are not used.

Frozen inputs: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=14d/hero-vllm-hillclimb/inputs/cases-0baf4938.json` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D14d%2Fhero-vllm-hillclimb%2Finputs%2Fcases-0baf4938.json)). Per-run outputs (`gates.json`, `long.json`, `load.json`, vLLM logs): `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=14d/hero-vllm-hillclimb/runs/` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D14d%2Fhero-vllm-hillclimb%2Fruns%2F)). These prefixes expire 14 days after writing. Code: research branch [`mcwitt/vllm-hillclimb`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/mcwitt/vllm-hillclimb), `experiments/evaluation/hero_vllm_hillclimb/` (multi-host DP serving on Iris, probes, grading, JAX reference). ## Correctness gates (v4)

The JAX reference is Levanter scoring the same `step-400407` checkpoint in placed order: BF16 weights, fp32 log-softmax, zero dropped MoE assignments, and a router bias that matches the export to 2.4e-7. It covers 11,370 positions in 32 fixed histories (GSM8K chat prompts and book excerpts, 40–1,835 tokens), plus 4K, 32K and 65K book histories (last 512 positions and every 256th). Outputs: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=14d/hero-vllm-hillclimb/reference/ref-a4/` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D14d%2Fhero-vllm-hillclimb%2Freference%2Fref-a4%2F)).

- (a) Hard: prompt scoring on DP engine 0 is bitwise identical across three passes within one server instance: alone, while the other 15 engines decode 8 requests each, and alone again.
- (b) Hard: the per-position maximum probability error of vLLM's top-5 against the JAX top-64 stays inside the control band for p50, p90, p99 and the fraction above 0.075, on both the short histories and the long histories. The band is the union of per-run 95% bootstrap intervals (whole histories resampled) over 5 control runs. Band, short histories: p90 [0.018, 0.034], p99 [0.066, 0.114], fraction above 0.075 [0.7%, 2.5%]. Band, long histories: p90 [0.022, 0.026], p99 [0.049, 0.069].
- (c) Decode non-regression against the control, distributional.
- (d) The decode load-dependence defect below is measured for every candidate. A change in it is called only after repeats.
- (e) From R12 on: decode self-consistency. The 32 gate histories are greedy-decoded for 256 tokens, alone on engine 0 and then 32 per engine on all 16 engines at once. Each prompt plus continuation is then scored by prefill on the same engine. The per-token difference |p_decode − p_prefill| of the chosen token (p50, p90, p99, maximum, fraction above 0.075) must stay at the control's level on the same nodes. Gate (b) covers prefill only; (e) covers the decode path, which can execute differently (for example, in full CUDA graphs).
- CUDA graphs must be captured; a run aborts if vLLM resolves `cudagraph_mode` to NONE.

An absolute 0.075 maximum is not used. At 11,370 positions the control itself reaches 0.50 at near-tie positions. Cross-run bitwise equality is also not used: fresh compiles of an unchanged config differ (see below).

## Results

"In flight" is the number of requests the server is processing at once (the closed-loop concurrency of the load generator, across all 16 GPUs). It is not a context length. Every row uses the same sequences of about 1,100 tokens (a 70-token prompt plus 1,024 sampled output tokens), except R10 and R11, which generate 4,096 output tokens. Throughput is output tokens/s per GPU. Each candidate ran back to back with its control on the same 4 nodes.

Decision rule: a candidate is decided on output tokens/s per GPU at 1,024 requests in flight (2,048 for the `max_num_seqs` 64 → 128 step and for the KV-bound 4K rows; 512 for rows that were swept only to 512). A change counts as a gain only beyond ±2%, the spread measured between same-node pairs that should be equal (the wheel pairs and the `max_num_seqs` pairs at 512 in flight). Latency columns are guardrails. Verdict words: "gain accepted" improves the deciding metric; "adopted, neutral" was taken for another reason with no measurable throughput effect; "no effect"; "rejected".

R0 is the mean of the `max_num_seqs` 32 controls measured on fast node sets, with the range and run count. No `max_num_seqs` 32 control was measured at 2,048 in flight on a fast node set, so that cell is blank.

## Known defects

- Open: decode is not invariant to load on other DP engines. Engine 0 decodes the same prompts alone, then while the other 15 engines are busy. Only 1–2% of its decode steps keep a bitwise-identical top-1 log-probability. Top-1 |Δp| reaches p90 0.013–0.016 and max 0.09–0.11 (0.16–0.20 nats); greedy tokens flip, once at a 0.43-nat margin. Load on engine 0 itself gives the same size of change. Repeated runs alone are bitwise identical, and prompt scoring (prefill) under peer load is bitwise identical. Both wheels show it. Mechanism measured (R18): DP padding runs every engine at the largest token count of any engine, so peer load moves engine 0 to a larger CUDA graph size; engine 0 stays bitwise unchanged while peers do not raise its padded size. A single capture size (`cudagraph_capture_sizes` = [`max_num_seqs`]) makes decode bitwise invariant to peer load, at a latency cost when engines are not full; dependence on engine 0's own batch remains, smaller.
- Fresh compiles of an unchanged config produce different numerics. Five compiles of `3004cd8` fell into three groups. Within a group, scoring is bitwise identical. Between groups, scoring differs at 99.5% of positions (|Δp| p99 0.072–0.075, max 0.48–0.56). The distributional statistics against JAX barely move: short-history p90 0.0270–0.0273, p99 0.0871–0.0885. Kernel autotuning or benchmarking at compile time is the suspected cause. Disabling Inductor's combo-kernel benchmarking did not remove the modes (R8), so the cause is still open.
- A Hero launch whose `--compilation-config` omits `vllm::grug_moe_short_conv` from `splitting_ops` runs without CUDA graphs. The fork's ShortConv guard sets `cudagraph_mode` to NONE with only a log line. Batch-1 decode was 182 ms/token against 56 ms with graphs.
- Open: three Triton kernels compile during serving instead of at startup (seen in the baseline and `0ac9dcb` server logs): `_causal_conv`, `fused_moe_kernel` and `_topk_log_softmax_kernel`. Inferred, not measured: the first requests that reach them pay the compile time. Fixed on a local fork branch (R28): no compile after startup, gates pass, no throughput change; a fork PR is drafted.
- Two GB200 node sets ran about 18–25% slower for both wheels: s76txs64, s9jtxs64, s7xsxs64, s8ltxs64 (rack 125) and s7psxs64, s96txs64, sbftxs64, sb3txs64 (rack 124). The cause is undetermined. With full CUDA graphs (R12) the gap disappears: single-request decode is 20.2–20.4 ms/token on a slow rack-122 set, a rack-125 set and a fast rack-394 set; the penalty is in the host-bound part of the PIECEWISE step (inferred).
- vllm#119 at `ef7f5a0` (the TP2/TP6 numbers in #11320) predates vllm#121, the position-dependent query scaling that export schema 3 requires. A merge onto `0ac9dcb` needed three fixes: allow Hero TP for schema 3, apply the TP2 NCCL guard to schema 3, and reshape Q by the per-rank head count in log scaling. Without the last, TP>1 crashes.

## Open questions

- The KV cache, not per-step time, caps the batch (R7): about 220 sequences per engine at 1K tokens and about 97 at 4K, from the fork's block accounting (4 attention groups at 16 tokens per block, with sliding-window groups holding every token below 2,048, plus 12 ShortConv state blocks). Fork changes could add about 12.5% (store 6 global KV heads instead of 12) and about 3% (ShortConv page padding). The 4K-output runs (R10, R11) matched the model: KV use was 31.7% at 32 sequences per engine and 47.2% at 48, and the cache filled with 96–128 sequences running per engine.
- The load generator stays below one core up to 4,096 requests in flight; four API servers lower TTFT but not throughput (R4b).
- Long-context parity is measured through 262K (R25): against two context-parallel JAX references, vLLM's scoring at 131K and 262K, including the log-scaled region past 65,536, agrees as well as at 65K.
- Throughput on long-context agentic traffic, where TP2 may help (#11320).

| Concurrency | Control tok/s/GPU | Candidate tok/s/GPU | Control TTFT p50 | Candidate TTFT p50 | Control ITL p50 | Candidate ITL p50 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 512 | 422 | 427 | 1.78 s | 0.99 s | 75.2 ms | 76.3 ms |
| 1024 | 425 | 852 | 77.6 s | 1.52 s | 75.2 ms | 74.3 ms |
| 2048 | 434 | 1,569 | 226 s | 2.95 s | 73.4 ms | 79.0 ms |
| 4096 | 425 | 492 | 537 s | 16.6 s | 75.1 ms | 485 ms |

KV accounting (corrected 2026-11-14 after tracing the fork's cache code at `0ac9dcb`): each engine's KV pool is about 63,500 blocks of 16 tokens, shared by 16 layer groups (1 global-attention, 3 sliding-window, 12 ShortConv state groups of 12 layers each). A sequence of L < 2,048 tokens holds ceil(L/16) blocks in each of the 4 attention groups, because sliding-window layers free nothing below the 2,048-token window, plus 12 ShortConv state blocks: 288 blocks at L = 1,094. That predicts 28% usage at 64 sequences and 58% at 128, matching the measured 27.7% and 53–55%, and a ceiling of about 220 sequences per engine. vLLM's reported 970,000-token capacity assumes 262,144-token requests, where the sliding-window groups are capped near 2K; at short L each token costs about 4 reported slots, which is where the earlier '3.7×' figure came from. Above 2K the sliding-window groups stop growing, so the ceiling at L = 4,096 is about 97 sequences per engine. Two fork-level inefficiencies remain: the global layers store KV for 12 heads although the model has 6 (about 12.5% of attention KV), and ShortConv state pages are padded to the attention page size (about 3% per sequence). No config flag reduces per-sequence use without changing numerics; more KV memory (`gpu_memory_utilization`) is the only config lever. vLLM logged no preemptions; at C4096 the engines oscillated between about 250 and 130 running requests. The load generator peaked at 70% of one core.

Gates v4: (a) pass; (b) vs-JAX p50 0.0019, p90 0.0273, p99 0.0897, fraction above 0.075 1.49%, long histories inside the band, pass. D1 maximum 0.170 against 0.111 (the recurring compile-mode value; not called).

Verdict: measured, not adopted. For 1,024-token rollouts the useful ceiling is about 128 sequences per engine (KV about 55%); 256 gains nothing at C2048 and fails at C4096. Longer rollouts lower the ceiling, but less than proportionally above 2K tokens (about 97 sequences per engine at 4K). Next: a 4K-output run to test that prediction, and `gpu_memory_utilization` as the one config-only KV lever. See row R7 in the issue body.

Verdict: for 4K outputs, 96 sequences per engine (1,536 in flight on 16 GPUs) runs at about 1,540 output tokens/s/GPU without waiting for KV; 128 adds 16% (0.90) to 20% (0.95) while KV-bound, at a higher TTFT. `gpu_memory_utilization` 0.95: gain accepted only for KV-bound loads, one pair, +3.6% (just above the ±2% pair noise); it leaves 5% less GPU memory for anything else in the process. See row R11 in the issue body.

comments.author: mcwitt-agent
comments.body:
🤖 R12: full CUDA graphs for decode. Letting uniform decode batches replay one full CUDA graph (`cudagraph_mode` FULL_AND_PIECEWISE) instead of piecewise graphs with eager ShortConv in between cuts the decode step 2.0–3.8× and raises throughput 43% at 1,024 in flight. All correctness gates pass, including a new decode-path gate (e). Two caveats: the gain at 2,048 in flight is only 2.5%, and long-prompt scoring got slower (65K: 9.5 → 12.7 s, cause unknown).

Question: the decode step is 56–78 ms from 1 to 128 sequences per engine, against a weight-read estimate of 4–5 ms. Where does the step go, and can a config or small fork change recover it?

Profile of the current step (torch profiler, `0ac9dcb`, PIECEWISE, 2 nodes DP8/EP8, 1 sequence per engine; profiling roughly doubles host time, so kernel durations are used, not host gaps):

- The GPU work is about 19 ms per step. Sum of all non-collective kernels: 17.1 ms (dense GEMMs 8.8, elementwise/norm 2.9, MoE expert GEMMs 2.9, memcpy 0.7, router 0.6, attention 0.4, ShortConv 0.4). Plus the minimum collective durations: 48 all-gathers at 22 µs and 48 reduce-scatters at 14 µs. At 32 per engine the same sum is about 38.5 ms; the MoE expert GEMM (18 ms) is then at the HBM roofline, because nearly every local expert is touched.
- The rest of the 56 ms step is host time. The GPU spends 75 of 103 profiled ms inside the 48 NCCL all-gathers, waiting for the slowest rank. The eager `vllm::grug_moe_short_conv` op runs 144 times per step (3 sites × 48 layers), and each call recomputes a flipped weight copy, clones its input and copies the output back. Each step also issues 434 `cudaMemcpyAsync`, about 580 kernel launches and 193 graph launches outside the graphs, plus a per-step gloo all-reduce for DP padding.
- The fork's guard allows only PIECEWISE mode when ShortConv is present; FULL modes are forced to NONE. The ShortConv metadata builder already declares uniform-batch full-graph support and pads its state indices into persistent buffers, as for Mamba layers.

Change: two guard relaxations in the vLLM fork, so that FULL_AND_PIECEWISE is accepted when `vllm::grug_moe_short_conv` is in `splitting_ops`. Uniform decode batches then replay one full graph; prefill and mixed batches keep the piecewise path. In `vllm/model_executor/models/config.py` (`GrugMoeForCausalLMConfig`), the early return now accepts `cudagraph_mode in (PIECEWISE, FULL_AND_PIECEWISE)` instead of only `PIECEWISE`. In `vllm/model_executor/models/grugmoe.py` (`_raise_for_unsupported_modes`), the same condition replaces `!= PIECEWISE`. This is not a fork PR yet. For the tests it ships as a Python overlay of the `0ac9dcb` aarch64 wheel: `overlay_wheel.py` replaces the two `.py` files and checks that the wheel's originals equal the `0ac9dcb` sources; compiled kernels are unchanged (overlay sha256 `38a6216d0334d2410ba878b0b6aec3e77f04adff4b17a690707823c57e31fa6b`). Config delta: `--compilation-config` with `"cudagraph_mode": "FULL_AND_PIECEWISE"`; `splitting_ops` and everything else unchanged. The resolved config in the engine log shows FULL_AND_PIECEWISE.

Runs: all on cw-us-east-08a, control and candidate back to back on the same nodes. The 2-node pair is Iris job `/mwittmann/hero-vllm-f1-fullgraph2n-20261114-082110` (rack 125, `max_num_seqs` 32, `gpu_memory_utilization` 0.95, which the 2-node layout needs). The 4-node per-step pair is `/mwittmann/hero-vllm-p1-profile4n-20261114-082245` (`max_num_seqs` 128), and the 4-node throughput pair is `/mwittmann/hero-vllm-t1-fullgraph-tput-20261114-090714` (`max_num_seqs` 128). Both 4-node jobs ran on the rack-122 set sfbsxs64, sgd50t64, sjwsxs64, sjxsxs64, which is slow: its control decodes a single request at 68.8 ms/token, against 56–58 ms on the fast sets. Code: [`6fc8d36355`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/6fc8d36355) for f1 and p1, [`f9c41edd93`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/f9c41edd93) for t1. Command for t1: `uv run python experiments/evaluation/hero_vllm_hillclimb/arm.py --direct --release 0ac9dcb --name t1-fullgraph-tput --sequence 0ac9dcb:mns128,0ac9dcb:fg128 --label-overlay fg128=<file holding the overlay wheel URL>:<sha256> --phases gates,decode,long,load --concurrencies 1024,2048`. Artifacts: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=14d/hero-vllm-hillclimb/runs/{f1-fullgraph2n-20261114-082110,p1-profile4n-20261114-082245,t1-fullgraph-tput-20261114-090714}-v{0,1}-…` (profiler traces under `profile/` in f1 and p1) ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D14d%2Fhero-vllm-hillclimb%2Fruns%2F)).

Per-step time: median inter-token latency on the same requests, measured in a 10 s window before the profiler starts. Every engine holds exactly the stated number of decoding sequences.

| Layout | Sequences per engine | PIECEWISE (control) | FULL_AND_PIECEWISE | Speedup |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 nodes, DP8/EP8 | 1 | 56.2 ms | 20.6 ms | 2.7× |
| 2 nodes, DP8/EP8 | 32 | 90.6 ms | 43.6 ms | 2.1× |
| 4 nodes, DP16/EP16 (slow set) | 1 | 89.9 ms | 23.4 ms | 3.8× |
| 4 nodes, DP16/EP16 (slow set) | 32 | 117.4 ms | 40.1 ms | 2.9× |
| 4 nodes, DP16/EP16 (slow set) | 128 | 112.9 ms | 55.5 ms | 2.0× |

With full graphs the profiler no longer slows the step (20.8 vs 20.6 ms), and the GPU is busy for the whole step. The FULL step on 4 nodes, in ms per step at 1 / 32 / 128 sequences per engine:

| Component | 1 | 32 | 128 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Step | 23.8 | 41.2 | 58.0 |
| MoE expert GEMMs (Triton `fused_moe`, default config) | 2.4 | 15.2 | 22.4 |
| Dense GEMMs (cuBLAS split-K at small M) | 8.5 | 10.2 | 10.3 |
| MoE all-gather + reduce-scatter | 7.7 | 8.3 | 10.6 |
| SiLU-and-mul activation | 0.2 | 1.3 | 4.7 |
| Elementwise and norms | 3.1 | 3.6 | 3.9 |
| Attention | 0.5 | 1.3 | 2.9 |
| Router | 0.6 | 0.7 | 0.8 |
| ShortConv kernel, plus about 1.7 ms of per-step weight flips and copies | 0.4 | 0.4 | 0.7 |
| Sampling and log-probs | <0.1 | <0.1 | <0.1 |

Throughput (t1, 4 nodes, slow set; 1,024 output tokens per request):

| Requests in flight (per engine) | Control tok/s/GPU | Candidate tok/s/GPU | Change | Control ITL p50 | Candidate ITL p50 | Control TTFT p50 | Candidate TTFT p50 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.91 | 3.02 | +230% | 68.8 ms | 20.4 ms | 0.15 s | 0.10 s |
| 1,024 (64) | 925 | 1,321 | +43% | 68.8 ms | 47.8 ms | 1.38 s | 1.58 s |
| 2,048 (128) | 1,701 | 1,744 | +2.5% | 74.0 ms | 59.7 ms | 2.55 s | 2.89 s |

Why the gain at 2,048 in flight is small (inferred, not yet tested): from the engines' 10 s stat lines, the steady step with 128 running is 59 ms against 77 ms for the control. But the candidate's engines spent much less of the window at 128 running sequences. That points to the request path (one API server, one load-generator process) not keeping up with about 35,000 streamed tokens/s, rather than to the step. A same-gang test with four API servers is next. A second possible contributor: any engine with a prefill in a step moves all 16 engines off the full graph for that step, and at 128 per engine refills are frequent.

Open defect of the candidate, cause unknown: long-prompt scoring is slower. 4K prompt 0.60 → 0.77 s, 32K 4.78 → 6.40 s, 65K 9.46 → 12.73 s (one pair). Prefill should still take the piecewise path; whether some prefill chunks take a different graph path, or the regression is capture or warmup cost, is being investigated.

Gates on t1: (a) pass (prompt scoring bitwise identical alone, under peer load and alone again). (b) short histories p50 0.0019, p90 0.0270, p99 0.0848, fraction above 0.075 1.41%; long histories p50 0.0072, p90 0.0248, p99 0.0543, fraction 0.47%; both inside the band, pass. D1 maximum 0.110 against 0.111. The 2-node and 4-node per-step pairs also pass (a) and (b). Gate (e), new (definition in the issue body): batched (32 per engine on all 16 engines, 131,072 tokens), |p_decode − p_prefill| of the chosen token has p50 0.0002, p90 0.0171, p99 0.0681, maximum 0.55, fraction above 0.075 0.81%; the control has 0.0003, 0.0175, 0.0704, 0.50, 0.88%. Alone on engine 0 (8,192 tokens): p99 0.0808 and maximum 0.45 against 0.0716 and 0.27, pass. Greedy decode against the same-node control diverges only at near-ties (26 of 32 cases, control top-2 margin at the divergence 0.004–0.36 nats; matched-prefix |Δp| p99 0.051, maximum 0.21). That is the pattern of a different numerics mode; two control compiles in different numerics modes give 26 of 32, p99 0.046, maximum 0.16.

Verdict: gain accepted for decode latency and for throughput at 1,024 in flight, pending the long-prompt regression. Not yet recommended for deployment: the long-prompt regression needs a cause, and the change needs a fork PR. Next on the same footing: a tuned GB200 fused-MoE config (1.26–1.53× faster per MoE layer at 128–2,048 gathered tokens in an offline search) and NCCL symmetric memory for the MoE collectives, both on top of full graphs. See row R12 in the issue body.

comments.author: mcwitt-agent
comments.body:
🤖 R12 follow-up: the long-prompt scoring regression reported for full CUDA graphs did not reproduce. In a second same-node pair with three repeats per prompt, PIECEWISE and FULL_AND_PIECEWISE score 32K and 65K prompts in the same time. The R12 numbers (65K 9.5 → 12.7 s) were single measurements, and the spread between repeats and between node sets is that large.

Question: does FULL_AND_PIECEWISE slow long-prompt prefill, and if so, is it a first-use cost (graph capture, warmup, JIT) or a slower steady path?

Method: on engine 0, each long prompt is first prefilled three times without log-probs (`max_tokens` 1), with the third pass under the torch profiler. It is then scored three times with top-5 prompt log-probs (the R12 measurement). Run: Iris job `/mwittmann/hero-vllm-t3a-longprof-20261114-101555` on cw-us-east-08a, 4 GB200 nodes, control (`max_num_seqs` 128, PIECEWISE) and candidate (FULL_AND_PIECEWISE overlay) back to back on the same nodes, code [`087be7776a`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/087be7776a), `--phases longprof`. The same repeats ran for FULL_AND_PIECEWISE in `/mwittmann/hero-vllm-t3b-api4-20261114-101607` on another node set. Artifacts: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=14d/hero-vllm-hillclimb/runs/{t3a-longprof-20261114-101555,t3b-api4-20261114-101607}-v{0,1}-…` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D14d%2Fhero-vllm-hillclimb%2Fruns%2F)).

| Prompt | PIECEWISE prefill, s (3 passes) | FULL prefill, s | PIECEWISE score with log-probs, s | FULL score with log-probs, s |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4K | 1.30, 0.42, 0.71 | 1.02, 0.37, 0.63 | 0.94, 0.78, 0.69 | 0.88, 0.63, 0.66 |
| 32K | 4.17, 4.19, 5.31 | 3.34, 3.53, 5.15 | 5.31, 5.13, 5.11 | 5.31, 5.14, 5.45 |
| 65K | 6.81, 6.67, 24.54 | 6.73, 6.76, 24.67 | 10.53, 11.04, 10.25 | 10.81, 10.56, 10.52 |

The third prefill pass ran under the profiler, which inflates it in both arms. On the other node set (t3b), FULL_AND_PIECEWISE scored the 65K prompt in 12.28, 10.72 and 11.74 s and prefilled it in 7.46, 6.47 and 7.10 s.

Two findings: there is no first-use or steady-state difference between the graph modes for prefill. Top-5 prompt log-probs add about 3.5–4.5 s to a 65K prompt, which is 50–65% of the 6.7 s prefill.

Verdict: the long-prompt regression is withdrawn as a defect of R12 (not reproduced; R12's long-prompt numbers were single measurements). R12's verdict no longer depends on it. The Known defects entry is removed and row R12's note updated.

comments.author: mcwitt-agent
comments.body:
🤖 R13: four API servers on top of full CUDA graphs. With the faster decode step (R12), one API server limits throughput at 2,048 requests in flight. Four API servers raise it 13% (1,830 → 2,072 output tokens/s/GPU) and cut TTFT p50 from 3.0 to 1.8 s; at 1,024 in flight the change is −2.4%. Same-step evidence: inter-token latency is unchanged (59.5 vs 59.4 ms).

Question: R12's candidate gained only 2.5% at 2,048 in flight although its step at 128 running sequences was 23% shorter. Is the request path (one API server process) the limit?

Config delta against the control: `--api-server-count 4` on the leader (control 1). Both arms use FULL_AND_PIECEWISE (the R12 overlay) and `max_num_seqs` 128. Run: Iris job `/mwittmann/hero-vllm-t3b-api4-20261114-101607` on cw-us-east-08a, 4 GB200 nodes, control and candidate back to back on the same nodes. Code [`087be7776a`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/087be7776a). Command: `uv run python experiments/evaluation/hero_vllm_hillclimb/arm.py --direct --release 0ac9dcb --name t3b-api4 --sequence 0ac9dcb:fg128,0ac9dcb:fg128api4 --label-overlay fg128=<overlay URL file>:<sha256> --label-overlay fg128api4=<same> --phases load,longrep --concurrencies 1024,2048`. Artifacts: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=14d/hero-vllm-hillclimb/runs/t3b-api4-20261114-101607-v{0,1}-…` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D14d%2Fhero-vllm-hillclimb%2Fruns%2F)).

| Requests in flight (per engine) | 1 API server tok/s/GPU | 4 API servers tok/s/GPU | Change | ITL p50 | TTFT p50 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 3.0 | 3.0 | 0% | 20.3 → 20.2 ms | 0.10 → 0.09 s |
| 1,024 (64) | 1,314 | 1,283 | −2.4% | 48.0 → 49.2 ms | 1.78 → 1.17 s |
| 2,048 (128) | 1,830 | 2,072 | +13% | 59.5 → 59.4 ms | 3.02 → 1.81 s |

CPU: with four API servers, each process peaks at one full core (mean 85–91%, maximum 100%), and the single load-generator process reaches 100% of a core at 2,048 in flight. The load generator is therefore the next limit at this rate (about 35,000 streamed tokens/s); the single-API-server process is not visible to the CPU sampler. In R14/R15's control (same config as this control, another run) the TTFT p90 at 2,048 in flight was 50 s while the engines' logs showed almost no waiting requests, so the wait was upstream of the engines.

Gates: not run in this job (an API server count does not change engine numerics); the long-prompt repeats are in the R12 follow-up.

Verdict: gain accepted for 2,048 in flight and above with full graphs (one pair, +13%); neutral at 1,024 (−2.4%, at the edge of pair noise). Throughput comparisons at 2,048 in flight from here on use four API servers. See row R13 in the issue body.

comments.author: mcwitt-agent
comments.body:
🤖 R14: a tuned GB200 config for the fused-MoE Triton kernel, on top of full CUDA graphs. Throughput at 1,024 in flight rises 7.3% (1,321 → 1,417 output tokens/s/GPU) and inter-token latency drops 7% (47.9 → 44.6 ms). There is no change at batch 1, as the kernel benchmark predicted. Gates pass.

Question: with full graphs, the MoE expert GEMMs are the largest part of the step at 32–128 sequences per engine (15.2 and 22.4 ms of 41 and 58 ms, R12). vLLM has no tuned config for this shape on GB200, so it uses `get_default_config`. Does a tuned config shorten the step?

Tuning: a search over 1,157 Triton configs (block M/N/K, group M, warps, stages) for the exact serving call: M gathered tokens (16 ranks × the batch per rank), top-8 over 384 experts, and an expert map that keeps the 24 local experts, hidden and intermediate size 3,072, BF16. Each config was timed by CUDA-graph replay on one GB200 node. Iris job `/mwittmann/hero-vllm-moe-tune-ep16-20261114-092249`; code [`31b73bed5e`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/31b73bed5e) (`moe_tune.py`, `moe_tune_kernel.py`). The resulting file is [`moe_configs/E=24,N=3072,device_name=NVIDIA_GB200.json`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/mcwitt/vllm-hillclimb/experiments/evaluation/hero_vllm_hillclimb/moe_configs/E%3D24%2CN%3D3072%2Cdevice_name%3DNVIDIA_GB200.json), keyed by M. vLLM picks the nearest key.

| Gathered tokens M (per-engine batch) | Default config, ms per MoE layer | Tuned, ms | Speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| 16 (1) | 0.102 | 0.097 | 1.05× |
| 128 (8) | 0.329 | 0.217 | 1.51× |
| 512 (32) | 0.389 | 0.273 | 1.42× |
| 1,024 (64) | 0.476 | 0.320 | 1.49× |
| 2,048 (128) | 0.569 | 0.451 | 1.26× |

Artifacts: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=14d/hero-vllm-hillclimb/runs/t2-fg-moe-symm-20261114-101057-v{0,1,2}-…` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D14d%2Fhero-vllm-hillclimb%2Fruns%2F)).

| Requests in flight (per engine) | Control tok/s/GPU | Tuned MoE tok/s/GPU | Change | ITL p50 | TTFT p50 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 3.0 | 3.0 | 0% | 20.4 → 20.6 ms | 0.08 → 0.08 s |
| 1,024 (64) | 1,321 | 1,417 | +7.3% | 47.9 → 44.6 ms | 1.42 → 1.39 s |

The 2,048 column is not attributed to the change: with one API server, both arms had a long TTFT tail at 2,048 in flight (p90 49.8 and 28.3 s) while the engines held almost no waiting requests (R13).

comments.author: mcwitt-agent
comments.body:
🤖 R16: the tuned MoE config (R14) and NCCL symmetric memory (R15) stacked on full CUDA graphs with four API servers, in an A/B/A run on a fast node set. Throughput rises 10.9% at 1,024 in flight (1,291 → 1,433 output tokens/s/GPU) and 14% at 2,048 (2,104 → 2,391). Single-request latency drops 8% (20.2 → 18.6 ms/token). All gates pass, and the two control runs agree within 0.6%.

Question: do R14 and R15 add up on top of R12 + R13, and do their single-pair gains repeat on another node set?

comments.author: mcwitt-agent
comments.body:
🤖 R18: the mechanism of D1, the dependence of decode numerics on load from other DP engines, is now measured rather than inferred. Engine 0's decode is bitwise unchanged as long as the peer engines do not raise the padded batch size above engine 0's own. It changes as soon as they do. With a single CUDA graph capture size, it is bitwise invariant to peer load at every load tested.

Question: is D1 caused by DP padding (every engine runs at the largest token count of any engine, so peer load changes engine 0's batch shape and with it the kernel choices)? R14 showed that the fused-MoE Triton block sizes do not change prefill arithmetic, which ruled out one candidate kernel. Does a single capture size remove D1?

Method (new `d1` phase; code [`57a652817e`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/57a652817e)): engine 0 greedy-decodes 8 fixed prompts (64 tokens) alone, then while every peer engine holds k = 1, 2, 8 and 16 requests, then alone again. Each pass is compared with the first alone pass, per token, on the top-1 log-probability. Three variants ran back to back on the same 2 GB200 nodes (DP8/EP8, `max_num_seqs` 32, `gpu_memory_utilization` 0.95): PIECEWISE (`0ac9dcb`), FULL_AND_PIECEWISE (R12 overlay), and FULL_AND_PIECEWISE with `cudagraph_capture_sizes` = [32] only, so every decode step pads to 32. Run: Iris job `/mwittmann/hero-vllm-d1a-2n-20261114-123134` on cw-us-east-08a. Command: `uv run python experiments/evaluation/hero_vllm_hillclimb/arm.py --direct --hosts 2 --release 0ac9dcb --name d1a-2n --sequence 0ac9dcb:mns32prof95,0ac9dcb:fg32prof95,0ac9dcb:fg32cap1_95 --label-overlay fg32prof95=<overlay URL file>:<sha256> --label-overlay fg32cap1_95=<same> --phases gates,d1 --d1-peer-loads 1,2,8,16`. Artifacts: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=14d/hero-vllm-hillclimb/runs/d1a-2n-20261114-123134-v{0,1,2}-…` (`d1.json`) ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D14d%2Fhero-vllm-hillclimb%2Fruns%2F)).

Engine 0 at one request; tokens whose top-1 log-probability is bitwise equal to the first alone pass (maximum |Δp|, greedy divergences in 8 cases):

| Peer load (requests per peer engine) | PIECEWISE | FULL_AND_PIECEWISE | FULL_AND_PIECEWISE, one capture size |
|---|---|---|---|
| alone again | 512/512 | 512/512 | 512/512 |
| 1 | 512/512 | 512/512 | 512/512 |
| 2 | 8/447 (0.058, 3) | 10/424 (0.096, 3) | 512/512 |
| 8 | 11/458 (0.142, 1) | 11/410 (0.090, 3) | 512/512 |
| 16 | 11/458 (0.142, 1) | 11/410 (0.090, 3) | 512/512 |

Findings:

- Peers at one request leave engine 0 at padded size 1, and its decode is bitwise unchanged. Peers at two move engine 0 to padded size 2, and 98% of its tokens change.
- Peer loads 8 and 16 give results bitwise identical to each other in both piecewise and full-graph modes. So the arithmetic depends on the padded size through a few kernel-choice thresholds (one between 2 and 8, none between 8 and 16), not on every size.
- With a single capture size, every step pads to 32 whatever the peers hold, and engine 0 is bitwise invariant to peer load. The gate's D1 measure is 0.000 (control: maximum 0.142).
- Load on engine 0 itself (8 requests sharing its batch) still changes its numerics with one capture size, but less: 247 of 512 tokens bitwise equal, maximum |Δp| 0.058 and no greedy divergence, against 7 of 410–418, 0.09–0.13 and 3 divergences without it. The remaining dependence is on engine 0's own batch composition, not on the padded size (inferred: per-request attention and ShortConv metadata).

Gates for the single-capture-size variant: (a) pass; (b) short histories p50 0.0021, p90 0.0270, p99 0.0869, fraction above 0.075 1.45%, pass. Its cost was not measured. Every decode step runs the 32-token graph, so at low load it should cost about the difference between the 1- and 32-sequence steps (20.6 vs 43.6 ms on this layout, R12; inferred). Near full batch it should cost nothing.

Verdict: D1's mechanism is identified as DP padding selecting a different CUDA graph size; a single capture size equal to `max_num_seqs` removes the dependence on peer load. That is a config-only option for uses that need it (for example, RL rollouts that want batch invariance), at a latency cost when engines are not full. D1 stays a known defect of the default configuration. The Known defects entry is updated.

Question: with full graphs, each decode step still recomputes a flipped and transposed copy of every ShortConv weight (144 per step), clones its input and copies the result back through `vstack`. That is about 1.7 ms of kernels per step in the R12 profile. How much of it can be removed?

- For pure-decode batches, ShortConv writes its update in the output buffer directly, instead of a clone plus a `vstack` copy. Same kernels and arithmetic.
- The flipped conv weight is computed once and cached. Measurement only: the cache is stale if weights change in place afterwards (RL weight publication), and under full graphs a refresh would also have to happen outside the captured step.

comments.author: mcwitt-agent
comments.body:
🤖 R23: rollout log-prob consistency, comparing one CUDA graph capture size with batch-invariant mode, on top of the full stack. They buy different kinds of consistency at very different cost.

- **One capture size** (`cudagraph_capture_sizes` = [128]) makes decode bitwise invariant to load on other engines and nearly invariant to the engine's own batch. Decode still differs from prefill scoring as much as by default. It costs 2.4% at 2,048 in flight (128 per engine) and 17% at 1,024, but 61% at 16 in flight, and single-request decode is 3.3× slower.
- **Batch-invariant mode** (`VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1`) additionally makes decode log-probs bitwise equal to prefill scoring of the same tokens. It costs 78% of throughput at every load measured and 7× the single-request latency (133.5 ms/token, close to the 117 ms/token of the Hero RL qualification run).

Question: R18 found that a single capture size removes D1. For RL rollouts, is that a cheaper route to rollout log-prob consistency than the fork's batch-invariant mode, which the Hero RL qualification run used? What does each cost at rollout batch sizes?

Variants, back to back on the same 4 GB200 nodes, all with the R16 stack (FULL_AND_PIECEWISE overlay, tuned MoE config, NCCL symmetric memory, four API servers) and `max_num_seqs` 128:

- A: default capture sizes.
- B: `cudagraph_capture_sizes` = [128], so every decode step pads to 128.
- C: `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1` with default capture sizes, as the qualification run used it. In this fork it also turns off symmetric-memory collectives and fused all-reduce paths.

Load: the RL-like closed loop (70-token prompts, 1,024 sampled tokens per request), 4 load-generator processes. Run: Iris job `/mwittmann/hero-vllm-rl1-capbi-20261114-135647` on cw-us-east-08a. Code [`0089b71e1f`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/0089b71e1f). Command: `uv run python experiments/evaluation/hero_vllm_hillclimb/arm.py --direct --release 0ac9dcb --name rl1-capbi --sequence 0ac9dcb:fg128stack,0ac9dcb:fg128stackcap1,0ac9dcb:fg128stackbi --label-overlay <each label>=<overlay URL file>:<sha256> --phases gates,decode,d1,load --concurrencies 16,512,1024,2048 --client-processes 4`. Artifacts: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=14d/hero-vllm-hillclimb/runs/rl1-capbi-20261114-135647-v{0,1,2}-…` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D14d%2Fhero-vllm-hillclimb%2Fruns%2F)).

Output tokens/s per GPU (ITL p50, TTFT p50):

| Requests in flight (per engine) | A: default sizes | B: one capture size | C: batch-invariant |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 3.31 (18.6 ms, 0.08 s) | 1.00 (62.0 ms, 0.14 s) | 0.46 (133.5 ms, 0.32 s) |
| 16 (1) | 43.4 (22.8 ms) | 16.9 (58.9 ms), −61% | 6.8 (150.8 ms), −84% |
| 512 (32) | 866 (36.7 ms) | 577 (54.9 ms), −33% | 179 (178.7 ms), −79% |
| 1,024 (64) | 1,446 (43.8 ms) | 1,203 (52.7 ms), −17% | 323 (197.2 ms), −78% |
| 2,048 (128) | 2,421 (51.2 ms) | 2,364 (52.7 ms), −2.4% | 532 (235.5 ms), −78% |

Consistency, engine 0 decoding 8 fixed prompts (64 greedy tokens each). "Peer load" means the other 15 engines hold k requests each; "own batch" means 8 more requests share engine 0's batch. Bitwise means the top-1 log-probability is identical to the first alone pass.

| | A: default sizes | B: one capture size | C: batch-invariant |
|---|---|---|---|
| Peer load k = 1 / 2 / 8 / 32: bitwise | 100% / 2% / 2% / 2% | 100% / 100% / 100% / 100% | 100% / 100% / 100% / 100% |
| Own batch: bitwise (max \|Δp\|, greedy flips) | 5/351 (0.094, 3) | 420/512 (0.0001, 0) | 512/512 (0, 0) |
| (e) decode vs prefill, batched 131,072 tokens: p99 \|Δp\| | 0.0687 | 0.0689 | 0.0000 |
| (e) alone, 8,192 tokens: p99 \|Δp\| | 0.0680 | 0.0632 | 0.0000 |

Gates (a) and (b) pass for B and C (short histories p99 0.0884 and 0.0877, fractions above 0.075 1.43% and 1.53%). The D1 measure is 0.000 for both, against 0.094 for A.

Answer to the question:

- If rollouts need reproducibility independent of what the other engines are doing (for example, re-sampling a group with identical log-probs), a single capture size gives it nearly for free when every engine runs a full batch (−2.4% at 128 per engine). It is expensive whenever engines run partly empty (−17% at 64 per engine, −61% at 1 per engine).
- If the rollout log-probs must equal what the trainer computes by scoring the same tokens (decode equal to prefill), only batch-invariant mode provides that here, at about 4.5× less throughput. A single capture size does not help with that.
- A capacity estimate for RL rollouts on 16 GPUs at 64–128 per engine: default about 1,450–2,420, single capture size about 1,200–2,360, batch-invariant about 320–530 output tokens/s/GPU.

This is one gang; a repeat in reverse order (C, B, A) is running on another node set, and its batch-invariant arm so far matches within 1% (133.5 vs 134.3 ms/token single request; 178.7 vs 178.0 tok/s/GPU at 512 in flight). See row R23 in the issue body.
