comments.author: mcwitt-agent
comments.body:
🤖 R24: long-prompt serving with the recommended stack at 32K and 65K, and the 8,192-token prefill budget re-tested on that load.

- With the stack, a single 65K prompt prefills at about 11,500 tokens/s (TTFT 5.7 s). Decode after it runs at 19 ms/token.
- With 4 long requests per engine (64 in flight), decode slows to 41 ms/token at 32K and 65 ms/token at 65K. Output throughput is 68 and 39 tokens/s/GPU for 1,024-token outputs.
- `max_num_batched_tokens` 8,192 cuts single-request TTFT by 38–52% (65K: 5.7 → 3.5 s; 32K: 3.6 → 1.7 s). It leaves throughput under load unchanged. With short outputs under load, it stretches inter-token latency to 1.1–2.0 s, because decode steps wait behind 8K-token prefill chunks.

Question (Matt's long-context metric): what does the recommended stack deliver on long prompts? Prefill rate, time to first token, decode speed after a long prefill, and throughput at concurrencies that fit the KV cache. Does the larger prefill budget, rejected for short prompts (R6), help here?

Load (new `longload` phase, [`3f52b30a90`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/3f52b30a90)):

- Prompts are distinct windows of a 262K-token book, 32,768 or 65,536 tokens long. Prefix caching is off.
- Outputs are 16 or 1,024 sampled tokens.
- Each point runs one request alone, then one closed-loop wave of 1 and 4 requests per engine (16 and 64 in flight). Requests are placed by the server's load balancer, not pinned to engines.

KV model: one sequence needs about 2,500 blocks at 32K+1K and 4,600 at 65K+1K, against about 63,500 per engine. So about 25 and 13 sequences fit per engine; 4 per engine fits with room.

Both arms run the R16 stack with `max_num_seqs` 128 (FULL_AND_PIECEWISE overlay, tuned MoE config, NCCL symmetric memory, four API servers); the candidate adds `--max-num-batched-tokens 8192` (control 2,048). Run: Iris job `/mwittmann/hero-vllm-L1-longctx-20261114-174010` on cw-us-east-08a, 4 GB200 nodes, control then candidate on the same nodes. Command: `uv run python experiments/evaluation/hero_vllm_hillclimb/arm.py --direct --release 0ac9dcb --name L1-longctx --sequence 0ac9dcb:fg128stack,0ac9dcb:fg128stackmbt8k --label-overlay <each label>=<overlay URL file>:<sha256> --phases longload --long-load-lengths 32768,65536 --long-load-outputs 16,1024 --long-load-per-engine 1,4`. Artifacts: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=14d/hero-vllm-hillclimb/runs/L1-longctx-20261114-174010-v{0,1}-…` (`longload.json`) ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D14d%2Fhero-vllm-hillclimb%2Fruns%2F)).

Single request (prefill budget 2,048 → 8,192):

| Prompt + output | TTFT | Prefill tokens/s | Decode ITL p50 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 32K + 1,024 | 3.55 → 1.69 s | 9,241 → 19,376 | 19.0 → 18.8 ms |
| 65K + 1,024 | 5.67 → 3.53 s | 11,565 → 18,548 | 19.4 → 19.0 ms |

Under load (1,024-token outputs; output tokens/s per GPU, TTFT p50, ITL p50; prefill budget 2,048 → 8,192):

| Prompt | 1 per engine (16 in flight) | 4 per engine (64 in flight) |
|---|---|---|
| 32K | 29.8 → 28.9 tok/s/GPU; TTFT 6.6 → 5.9 s; ITL 26.8 → 28.7 ms | 67.6 → 64.2; TTFT 26.3 → 25.7 s; ITL 40.6 → 42.8 ms |
| 65K | 22.1 → 21.5; TTFT 16.0 → 15.0 s; ITL 29.0 → 31.6 ms | 38.9 → 39.7; TTFT 52.9 → 50.9 s; ITL 65.2 → 64.1 ms |

With 16-token outputs (a prefill-dominated load) at 4 per engine, ITL p50 is 524 ms (2,048) against 1,105 ms (8,192) at 32K, and 523 against 2,012 ms at 65K: decode steps wait behind prefill chunks.

Notes:

- Under load, TTFT is much larger than the single-request prefill time (16 s at 1 per engine and 65K). Requests are not pinned, so some engines hold two prefills while others idle. Long prefills also run eagerly in lockstep with every other engine (inferred).
- Output tokens are a small share of the work here: at 65K × 64 in flight, the prompts carry about 4.2M tokens against 66K output tokens.
- 131K and 262K throughput will follow once their correctness gate (running) passes.

Verdict: the 8,192 prefill budget is a TTFT lever for single long prompts (−38% to −52%). It does not raise long-prompt throughput, and it hurts decode latency for mixed short-output traffic, so it is not adopted as a default. See row R24 in the issue body.

comments.author: mcwitt-agent
comments.body:
🤖 R25: long-context correctness. Gate (b) passes at 131K and 262K tokens, where the export's log-scaled query scaling is active (`log_scaling_n_floor` 65,536), for both PIECEWISE and the recommended stack. vLLM's error against JAX past position 65,536 is about as far above the JAX-vs-JAX spread as below it, so there is no sign of a log-scaling defect.

Question: no gate had exercised positions past 65,536, where Hero's log scaling starts. Do vLLM and JAX agree there, at 131K and 262K?

JAX references: the replicated layout used for ref-a4 cannot hold a 262K history. `reference_hero.py` now scores long histories one at a time with the sequence sharded over a context axis ([`95e705902a`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/95e705902a)). Two independent layouts ran:

- CP32 on 8 GB200 nodes (`ref-cp32-a1`).
- CP16 on 4 GB200 nodes (`ref-cp16-a1`).

Both use BF16 weights and fp32 log-softmax, with 0 dropped MoE assignments. Each covers the 65K, 131K and 262K prefixes of one book: the last 512 positions plus every 256th, so 766, 1,022 and 1,534 positions. At 65K, CP32 rates vLLM the same as ref-a4 does (p50/p90/p99/fraction above 0.075: 0.0071/0.0228/0.0483/0.0013 against 0.0075/0.0254/0.0480/0.0013).

vLLM: Iris job `/mwittmann/hero-vllm-G1-long262k-20261114-175334` on cw-us-east-08a, 4 GB200 nodes, PIECEWISE (`max_num_seqs` 128) then the R16 stack, each scoring the three histories on engine 0 with top-5 prompt log-probs. Both arms return bitwise-identical scores, because prefill takes the same path. At 262K vLLM scores 262,143 tokens: Hero's limit of 262,144 includes the sampled token. Code [`4c07bb4316`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/4c07bb4316). Artifacts: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=14d/hero-vllm-hillclimb/runs/G1-long262k-20261114-175334-v{0,1}-…` and `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=14d/hero-vllm-hillclimb/reference/{ref-cp32-a1,ref-cp16-a1}/` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D14d%2Fhero-vllm-hillclimb%2F)).

Per-position maximum probability error (the gate (b) statistic), vLLM against CP32, all positions:

| History | Positions | p50 | p90 | p99 | max | Fraction above 0.075 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 65K | 766 | 0.0071 | 0.0228 | 0.0483 | 0.125 | 0.13% |
| 131K | 1,022 | 0.0068 | 0.0251 | 0.0562 | 0.289 | 0.59% |
| 262K | 1,533 | 0.0080 | 0.0255 | 0.0511 | 0.131 | 0.33% |

Against the long-history band (p50 [0.0061, 0.0075], p90 [0.0219, 0.0260], p99 [0.0488, 0.0688], fraction [0.05%, 0.72%]), every statistic is inside except the 262K p50 (0.0080). By region, with the two JAX layouts against each other as the scale:

| History, positions | JAX CP16 vs CP32: p50 / p90 / p99 | vLLM vs CP16 | vLLM vs CP32 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 262K, below 65,536 | 0.0057 / 0.0203 / 0.0452 | 0.0068 / 0.0236 / 0.0467 | 0.0061 / 0.0243 / 0.0500 |
| 262K, 65,536–131,071 | 0.0077 / 0.0227 / 0.0515 | 0.0076 / 0.0256 / 0.0597 | 0.0085 / 0.0285 / 0.0704 |
| 262K, 131,072 and above | 0.0071 / 0.0210 / 0.0509 | 0.0083 / 0.0251 / 0.0585 | 0.0082 / 0.0247 / 0.0511 |
| 131K, 65,536–131,071 | 0.0059 / 0.0198 / 0.0538 | 0.0071 / 0.0242 / 0.0576 | 0.0070 / 0.0253 / 0.0596 |

The two JAX layouts themselves differ a little more beyond 65,536 than below it. vLLM's distance to JAX keeps the same margin above that spread in every region (about 0.001 at p50 and 0.003–0.006 at p90), and nothing grows with length. The 131K maximum of 0.29 is at one position where CP32 also differs from CP16 by 0.30.

Verdict: pass. vLLM's long-context scoring through 262K, including the log-scaled region, agrees with JAX as well as it does at 65K. The 262K p50 sits 0.0005 above a band measured at 65K, which is inside the spread between the two JAX layouts. The open question about 131K/262K parity in the issue body is closed.

comments.author: mcwitt-agent
comments.body:
🤖 R26: TP2/DP8 with full CUDA graphs on 32K and 65K prompts. It is correct and gives lower per-request latency at a given number of requests per GPU. On this load it lies on about the same throughput–latency curve as the TP1/DP16 stack, so no 2× gain appears here. Single-prompt prefill is unchanged (65K: 7.6 s against 7.9 s).

Question: R5 rejected TP2 for short-prompt rollouts. Is it a win for long prompts with full graphs, as reported for agentic traffic (#11320)?

Candidate: TP2/DP8/EP16 on an overlay of the vllm#119 TP2 wheel (R5) plus the R12 guard relaxation. It uses FULL_AND_PIECEWISE (confirmed in the engine log), `max_num_seqs` 128, and the NCCL settings from vllm#119 (no custom or symmetric-memory all-reduce, no fused all-reduce passes). Control: the R16 stack at TP1/DP16. Load as in R24 (book windows of 32K or 65K tokens; 16 or 1,024 sampled tokens). Per-engine counts are per DP engine, so the candidate's 1 and 4 per engine are 8 and 32 requests in flight, against 16 and 64 for the control. Run: Iris job `/mwittmann/hero-vllm-L2-tp2fg-20261114-175345` on cw-us-east-08a, 4 GB200 nodes, control then candidate on the same nodes. Code [`92e3720a08`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/92e3720a08) and later. Command: `uv run python experiments/evaluation/hero_vllm_hillclimb/arm.py --direct --release 0ac9dcb --name L2-tp2fg --sequence 0ac9dcb:fg128stack,0ac9dcb:tp2fg --label-overlay fg128stack=<R12 overlay URL file>:<sha256> --label-overlay tp2fg=<TP2+R12 overlay URL file>:<sha256> --phases gates,decode,longload --long-load-lengths 32768,65536 --long-load-outputs 16,1024 --long-load-per-engine 1,4`. Artifacts: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=14d/hero-vllm-hillclimb/runs/L2-tp2fg-20261114-175345-v{0,1}-…` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D14d%2Fhero-vllm-hillclimb%2Fruns%2F)).

1,024-token outputs (output tokens/s per GPU; TTFT p50; ITL p50):

| Prompt | TP1/DP16, 16 in flight | TP1/DP16, 64 in flight | TP2/DP8, 8 in flight | TP2/DP8, 32 in flight |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 32K | 29.1; 7.4 s; 26.8 ms | 67.4; 26.3 s; 40.7 ms | 21.1; 3.9 s; 19.9 ms | 51.9; 11.3 s; 30.3 ms |
| 65K | 25.8; 18.0 s; 21.1 ms | 41.9; 52.8 s; 58.2 ms | 18.2; 7.6 s; 20.0 ms | 36.4; 23.2 s; 38.1 ms |

Single request (TP1 → TP2): 32K TTFT 3.97 → 3.53 s; 65K 7.92 → 7.56 s; decode ITL about 18–19 ms in both.

Gates for TP2 with full graphs: (a) pass; (b) short histories p50 0.0021, p90 0.0278, p99 0.0913, fraction above 0.075 1.61%, pass; (e) batched p99 0.0687 against 0.0679, pass.

Verdict: correct, but no throughput gain on this long-prompt load at matched latency (one pair, on a node set where the TP1 control prefilled at 8,300 tokens/s against 11,500 in R24). TP2 halves the requests per engine, so it fits fewer long sequences per GPU group and offers lower latency at a given load. It is an option for latency-bound long-context serving; R5 already rejected it for throughput. The reported 2× on agentic traffic likely depends on traffic shape (multi-turn prefix reuse, prompt mix) that this load does not have (inferred). See row R26 in the issue body.

comments.author: mcwitt-agent
comments.body:
🤖 R27: long-prompt serving at 131K and 258K tokens with the recommended stack, after R25's correctness pass at those lengths.

- A single request prefills at about 10,300–11,500 tokens/s at every length from 32K to 258K (258K TTFT 25 s). Decode right after the prefill runs at 20–21 ms/token.
- At 2 such requests per engine (32 in flight), output throughput is 18 (131K) and 10 (258K) tokens/s/GPU for 1,024-token outputs, at 71 and 118 ms/token. TTFT is dominated by queueing behind other prefills.
- The 8,192-token prefill budget cuts single-request TTFT by 26–31% here and leaves loaded throughput within ±9%.

Load and setup as in R24, with 131,072- and 258,048-token windows of the book. The longest stays below Hero's 262,144-token limit with room for 4,096 output tokens. Requests run at 1 and 2 per engine (16 and 32 in flight). The KV model gives about 8,400 blocks per 131K sequence and 16,600 per 258K sequence, against about 63,500 per engine: 7 and 3 sequences fit per engine. Run: Iris job `/mwittmann/hero-vllm-L3-longctx256-20261114-181638` on cw-us-east-08a, 4 GB200 nodes, the R16 stack with prefill budget 2,048 (control) then 8,192 on the same nodes. Code [`4c07bb4316`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/4c07bb4316). Command: `uv run python experiments/evaluation/hero_vllm_hillclimb/arm.py --direct --release 0ac9dcb --name L3-longctx256 --sequence 0ac9dcb:fg128stack,0ac9dcb:fg128stackmbt8k --label-overlay <each label>=<overlay URL file>:<sha256> --phases longload --long-load-lengths 131072,258048 --long-load-outputs 16,1024 --long-load-per-engine 1,2`. Artifacts: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=14d/hero-vllm-hillclimb/runs/L3-longctx256-20261114-181638-v{0,1}-…` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D14d%2Fhero-vllm-hillclimb%2Fruns%2F)).

Single request (prefill budget 2,048 → 8,192):

| Prompt + output | TTFT | Prefill tokens/s | Decode ITL p50 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 131K + 1,024 | 11.35 → 7.81 s | 11,547 → 16,791 | 19.7 → 19.8 ms |
| 258K + 1,024 | 24.93 → 18.56 s | 10,349 → 13,900 | 20.9 → 20.8 ms |

Under load, 1,024-token outputs (output tokens/s per GPU; TTFT p50 / p90; ITL p50; prefill budget 2,048 → 8,192):

| Prompt | 1 per engine (16 in flight) | 2 per engine (32 in flight) |
|---|---|---|
| 131K | 14.3 → 15.3; 34.0 / 46.3 → 30.2 / 41.9 s; 35.3 → 35.6 ms | 18.2 → 18.3; 71.7 / 72.1 → 62.5 / 74.7 s; 71.3 → 73.5 ms |
| 258K | 8.2 → 8.9; 66.9 / 98.4 → 65.8 / 87.6 s; 54.3 → 47.7 ms | 10.1 → 9.8; 140.4 / 142.0 → 139.1 / 141.8 s; 118.4 → 91.5 ms |

With 16-token outputs under load, the 8,192 budget again stretches inter-token latency (for example 0.17 → 0.96 s at 131K, 1 per engine), as in R24.

Summary of the long-context measurements (R24, R27; recommended stack, 16 GB200 GPUs):

| Prompt | Single-request TTFT | Decode after prefill | Sequences that fit per engine (KV model) | Output tok/s/GPU at the load measured (1,024-token outputs) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 32K | 3.6 s | 19 ms | ~25 | 68 at 4 per engine |
| 65K | 5.7 s | 19 ms | ~13 | 39 at 4 per engine |
| 131K | 11.4 s | 20 ms | ~7 | 18 at 2 per engine |
| 258K | 24.9 s | 21 ms | ~3 | 10 at 2 per engine |

Verdict: the stack serves Hero through 258K tokens, with prefill near 11K tokens/s per engine and decode near 20 ms/token after the prefill. Under concurrent long prompts, throughput is bounded by prefill and TTFT by queueing. The 8,192 prefill budget remains a TTFT lever for long-prompt-only traffic, not a default. See row R27 in the issue body.

comments.author: mcwitt-agent
comments.body:
🤖 R28: fixes for the three Triton kernels that compiled during serving. With them, the server logs no JIT compile after startup (0 warnings against 3 for the control), and gates (a), (b) and (e) pass. First-request latency shows no measurable change on these nodes.

Question: can the three serving-time compiles (`fused_moe_kernel`, `_topk_log_softmax_kernel`, `_causal_conv1d_fwd_kernel`; Known defects) be removed without changing numerics or throughput?

Changes (vLLM fork, local branch, not yet a fork PR):

- `fused_moe_kernel`: `do_not_specialize` on `EM` and `num_valid_tokens`. Odd gathered token counts no longer compile new variants. A startup warmup also runs each MoE config the server can select for 1 to `max_num_batched_tokens` × DP tokens.
- `_topk_log_softmax_kernel`: the sampler warmup compiles every top-k block size for 0 to `max_logprobs` log-probs, on the real logits.
- `_causal_conv1d_fwd_kernel`: the per-request metadata pointers no longer specialize on 16-byte alignment, so a mixed batch with a decode count that is not a multiple of 4 reuses the warm variant.

Each fix has a GPU test. All 4 pass on GB200. On the unmodified wheel, the causal-conv test fails on the real symptom: compiled variants [1, 2, 2, 2] instead of [1, 1, 1, 1]. The other two tests import the new warmup code, so they cannot run there.

Run: Iris job `/mwittmann/hero-vllm-j5-jitprewarm-20261114-203142` on cw-us-east-08a, 4 GB200 nodes, `0ac9dcb` with `max_num_seqs` 128 (PIECEWISE), control then candidate (a Python overlay of the branch) on the same nodes. Code [`7fcf1a04f5`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/7fcf1a04f5): a new `first` phase times the first requests after server-ready against the same requests repeated. Artifacts: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=14d/hero-vllm-hillclimb/runs/j5-jitprewarm-20261114-203142-v{0,1}-…` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D14d%2Fhero-vllm-hillclimb%2Fruns%2F)).

| | Control | With fixes |
|---|---|---|
| JIT-monitor compile warnings after startup | 3 (the three kernels) | 0 |
| Server ready | 431 s | 379 s |
| First / repeated greedy decode with top-2 log-probs (16 tokens) | 1.04 / 1.06 s | 0.94 / 0.96 s |
| First / repeated prompt scoring | 0.12 / 0.12 s | 0.12 / 0.13 s |
| First / repeated burst of 7 prompts during a decode (mixed batch) | 0.13 / 0.10 s | 0.13 / 0.13 s |
| Throughput at 512 in flight | 520 tok/s/GPU (ITL 60.7 ms) | 526 (60.3 ms) |

The monitor also fires on Triton disk-cache hits, and these nodes had warm caches, so the control's compiles cost little here (inferred). On a cold node they would cost a full Triton compile on the first request that reaches each variant.

Gates for the candidate: (a) pass; (b) short histories p50 0.0019, p90 0.0273, p99 0.0897, fraction above 0.075 1.49%, pass; (e) batched p99 0.0713 against 0.0679, pass.

Verdict: the fixes remove the serving-time compiles with no throughput change and passing gates. They are ready for a fork PR, which is drafted and awaits review. The Known defects entry is updated.

spillover_issues.author: RohithKuditipudi
spillover_issues.body:
A caller that runs `execute()` on a worker thread has no way, from any other thread, to make it stop early — whether the pipeline's results are no longer needed or the process is shutting down. If the worker job that `execute()` launches never schedules (no accelerator capacity), the call blocks for 12 hours and nothing can release it sooner.

What `execute()` launches: on a fresh context it calls `_start_pool()`, which submits a coordinator job (`execution.py:502`), tells it to spawn a worker job, and waits for the first worker to register — up to `ZEPHYR_WORKERS_READY_WAIT`, default 12 h (`execution.py:532-533`). The handles to these jobs are held in variables local to the call (`execution.py:646`); nothing is assigned to the context object, and `self._state` stays `NEW`.

What `shutdown()` does: it stops what the context has registered — the pool that only `start()` assigns (`execution.py:550`) — and returns immediately for state `NEW` (`execution.py:689`). During `execute()` it therefore has no effect: the jobs it would need to stop are reachable only from inside the blocked call. Calling `start()` first does not help: `start()` holds `_state_lock` across the same first-worker wait (`execution.py:550`), and `shutdown()` blocks acquiring that lock (`execution.py:684`).

What changed: before #7145, `execute()` stored its coordinator job on the instance (`self._coordinator_job`) and `shutdown()` terminated that job — workers included, via cascading termination — from any thread at any point in the call. #7145 moved the pool into the `execute()` call and rewrote `shutdown()` around the `NEW`/`OWNER` state machine; cancelling a running `execute()` was dropped with no replacement.

Observed in production, 2026-08-22/23: a driver needed to cancel `execute()` calls whose work other pools had already completed. The v5litepod worker jobs never scheduled (`Insufficient TPUs (need 4, available 0)`); `shutdown()` at ~02:00 UTC had no effect, and each blocked call held its thread until the 12 h wait expired at ~11:20 UTC. The only unstick was killing the coordinator jobs out-of-band.

Done when: `shutdown()` (or an equivalent) promptly cancels a running `execute()`, including one still waiting for its first worker. One shape: register the coordinator group on the context at creation, before the blocking waits; deregister when the pool ends; have `shutdown()` stop registered live groups regardless of state.

spillover_issues.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This eval experiment tried to reproduce Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index Terminal-Bench 2.1 scores on Marin for four large MoE baselines using Terminus 2, three attempts per task, a 250-turn limit, a 7,200-second agent timeout, and the pinned TB2.1 dataset. The main result is mixed. Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B A55B NVFP4 reproduced the AAII point estimate almost exactly at 54.09% versus 53.93%. Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-FP8 was still preliminary in the posted table, at 42.34% versus 47.57% with 110/111 completed trials and 156 trials remaining. DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 cleared the infrastructure-success gate but missed parity badly, scoring 56.23% versus AAII's 78.65% with no confirmed protocol discrepancy. GLM-5.2 AWQ INT4 produced no valid cohort because the checkpoint could not be served with the required context under the tested single-node geometry. The follow-up work is to finish Qwen, isolate the DeepSeek score gap, and rerun GLM with a serving geometry that preserves the intended context budget.

### Helpful links
- Experiment summary comment: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8261#issuecomment-5299403446
- Versioned launch configs and artifacts: https://huggingface.co/datasets/penfever/large-model-agentic-eval-parity-tb21-aa/tree/main/artifacts
- Baseline/context comment: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8261#issuecomment-5299504940
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Human Authored tl;dr

WHAT THIS IS: The purpose of this experiment was to try to reproduce AAII tb2.1 eval scores on the Marin cluster on some strong baselines.
WHY WE DID IT: Exercise Marin's eval pipeline and thoroughly understand how AAII executes tb2.1, since minor differences in protocol can dramatically impact scores.
RESULT: Picked four models; Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-FP8, DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731, Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B A55B NVFP4, GLM-5.2 AWQ INT4. GLM 5.2 did not run (needs either pipeline parallel or B200s or possibly both). Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B A55B NVFP4 succeeded. Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-FP8 is slightly below parity but pretty close. DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 is way below parity and there's no obvious discrepancy so I'm not sure why.

comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
🤖 ## Experiment summary

This experiment compares Marin's Terminal-Bench 2.1 results with the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (AAII) for four large MoE models. The protocol uses Terminus 2, three attempts per task (267 trials), a 250-turn limit, a 7,200-second agent timeout, and the pinned `terminal-bench/terminal-bench-2-1@sha256:7d7bdc1cbedad549fc1140404bd4dc45e5fd0ea7c4186773687d177ad3a0699a` dataset. Marin used Daytona sandboxes; AAII used E2B.

| Model | AAII | Marin | Delta | Scoreable trials | Infrastructure success | Status |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B A55B NVFP4 | 53.93% | 54.09% | +0.16 pp | 257/267 | 96.25% | Reproduced |
| Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-FP8 | 47.57% | 42.34% | -5.23 pp | 110/111 completed | 99.10% | Preliminary; 156 trials remain |
| DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 | 78.65% | 56.23% | -22.42 pp | 265/267 | 99.25% | Valid Marin result; parity failed |
| GLM-5.2 AWQ INT4 | 77.90% | — | — | 0/267 | 0.00% | No valid cohort |

The Qwen rerun aligns the 262,144-token serving context and 81,920-token generation limit across vLLM and Terminus 2. Its current 42.34% mean comprises 48 successes and 62 zeros. Thirteen `AgentTimeoutError` trials received verifier scores and are valid; one `VerifierTimeoutError` is an infrastructure failure.

Nemotron reproduces the AAII point estimate within 0.16 percentage points. DeepSeek clears the 90% infrastructure gate but remains 22.42 points below AAII with no confirmed protocol discrepancy. GLM did not produce a valid result because the AWQ checkpoint could not be served with the required context under the tested single-node geometry; pipeline parallelism or B200 capacity remains to be tested.

Checkpoint and environment differences limit the comparison. AAII evaluated unquantized Qwen and GLM checkpoints and BF16 Nemotron, while Marin used Qwen FP8, GLM AWQ INT4, and Nemotron NVFP4. DeepSeek used the same checkpoint family. The sandbox provider also differs.

Next steps are to finish the Qwen cohort, isolate the DeepSeek score gap, and rerun GLM with a serving geometry that preserves the intended context budget.

comments.body:
🤖 Official and independent baselines put these results in context:

| Model | Vendor SWE-Bench Verified | Vendor Terminal-Bench | Artificial Analysis TB 2.1 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Qwen3.5-122B-A10B | 72.0 | 49.4 (TB 2.0) | 47.57 |
| DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 | not reported | 82.7 (TB 2.1) | 78.65 |
| Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B A55B | 69.5 | 53.9 (TB 2.1) | 53.93 |
| GLM-5.2 | not reported | 81.0 (TB 2.1) | 77.90 |

Artificial Analysis v4.1.1 runs 89 tasks three times with Terminus-2 in E2B and reports pass@1. Only DeepSeek is an exact checkpoint match: its entry uses `DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731`; the other entries differ in precision or checkpoint from this campaign. Vendor conditions also vary. GLM reports 256K context and 48K maximum output with a four-hour timeout; NVIDIA documents thinking-mode sampling and an eight-repeat Terminal-Bench recipe, but its public recipe names TB 2.0 while the card reports TB 2.1; Qwen does not publish a complete resource-limit recipe. These figures are therefore comparison targets, not zero-confound parity baselines.

The official Terminal-Bench leaderboard did not contain any of the four exact campaign targets when checked on August 11, 2026. Current DeepSeek and GLM-5.2 model materials also do not report SWE-Bench Verified; older family results are not transferable to these checkpoints.
